Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.
  • Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.
  • In a recent development, surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

In a recent development, surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

According to recent reports, after Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Recent findings suggest that musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”.

Sources indicate that on Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

Sources indicate that as we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement states it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

According to recent reports, so Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Industry observers note that brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

The memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c.

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:.

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:.

It has been revealed that “It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”.

It has been revealed that that’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself indicates is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Recent findings suggest that besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

In a recent development, what do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

According to recent reports, you can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that two XRP Ledger lending amendments, LendingProtocol and LendingProtocolV1_1, each have 28 votes out of 35 validators, or 80%, according to XRPScan data on Thursday. Each of them needs one more vote to start a 14-day countdown to activation, according to XRPScan.

On Wednesday, the SingleAssetVault amendment reached 29 votes. According to XRPScan, its earliest activation date is Dec. 9, and its support has to stay above 80% until then.

XRP was trading at around $0.95 on Thursday, up 4.1% over 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap.

In a recent development, on Nov. 20, XRPScan demonstrated 25 votes for SingleAssetVault and 24 votes for each of the two lending amendments. Validators run by Interledger, onXRP, GateHub and Flare were among the last to vote for them.

RippleX opened LendingProtocolV1_1 for voting with a post on X on Sept. 30, when the amendment arrived with rippled version 3.4.0. "LendingProtocolV1_1 is open for validator voting. It introduces closed-ended vaults and cash-basis accounting for XRPL lending, and it must activate before LendingProtocol and SingleAssetVault can proceed," the RippleX developer account wrote.

J. Ayo Akinyele, head of engineering at RippleX, explained the role of the upgrade in a post on June 25. "v1.1 is an enhancement to the Lending Protocol, not a replacement for v1.0," he wrote, adding that "Lending on XRPL will evolve dynamically.".

In a recent development, ripple described the mechanics of the protocol on Nov. 19. "The upcoming XRP Ledger Lending Protocol is designed to bring loan issuance and repayment directly onto the ledger. Lenders deposit into a Single Asset Vault, and the Lending Protocol lets loan brokers use that capital to glitch loans and track repayments onchain," the tech giant wrote on X.

Ripple engineer Ed Hennis presented the protocol in a thread on X in December 2025. He called it a protocol-native system for "fixed-term, fixed-rate, underwritten credit." "XRP's $124B market cap can finally be lent into institutional credit facilities to generate real yield instead of sitting idle," Hennis wrote at the time.

Jazzi Cooper, head of product at RippleX, wrote on Sept. 11 that "XRP as collateral for institutional credit is a killer use case (and supported by xls65/66 lending protocol!)".

Recent findings suggest that on the same day, the XRP Ledger Foundation shared an interview with its chief technology officer, Denis Angell. "We are writing TradFi primitives into the XRP Ledger," Angell mentioned. In the interview, he compared the lending protocol to a closed-end fund, where investors put in XRP or RLUSD and receive interest.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 1Password confirmed a breach on the 25th of November after an attacker copied customer records through compromised backend systems.
  • According to recent reports, the company said password vaults remained protected, while the stolen information raised the risk of convincing impersonation attempts.
  • Recent findings suggest that 1Password began investigating on the 19th of November after an attacker compromised an employee’s corporate GitHub account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

1Password confirmed a breach on the 25th of November after an attacker copied customer records through compromised backend systems.

According to recent reports, the company said password vaults remained protected, while the stolen information raised the risk of convincing impersonation attempts. For those unaware, 1Password is a password manager that stores passwords, passkeys, and other sensitive information in encrypted digital vaults.

Recent findings suggest that 1Password began investigating on the 19th of November after an attacker compromised an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker used that access to push malicious code into backend services and download records for some customers.

Industry observers note that those included names, email addresses, account identifiers, creation and sign-in times, and non-secret technical metadata. The attacker also copied public keys, authentication parameters, and tokens from certain invitation, provisioning, and account recovery links.

1Password stated those tokens alone could not grant access; owners also needed to complete sign-in or email verification. The attacker also copied private source code and accessed the company’s software deployment systems.

However, it stated that it never stored account passwords or Secret Keys required to decrypt vaults.

Recent findings suggest that the organization disabled the compromised account and rotated potentially exposed credentials. It reported no internal evidence of account takeovers through exposed provisioning tokens.

The reassurance about vaults left a separate question hanging: how had one employee account enabled such extensive access?

Akash Network founder Greg Osuri said his trust was “heavily diminished” and called for an option to keep vaults entirely local. Crypto and blockchain CTO Nicki Sanders focused on the intrusion, stating,.

The part that worries me is how they got in.

Trading Strategy co-founder Mikko Ohtamaa favored open-source alternatives, arguing that transparency could make persistent attacks easier to detect.

Sources indicate that others were less categorical. X user Tom Lombardi called the incident,.

The disagreement extended to passwords themselves. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) urged users to change all passwords.

After 1Password noted passwords remained unexposed, CZ acknowledged the clarification and suggested weak-password checks and changing login emails to protect against phishing.

Stolen account details could help scammers impersonate 1Password through convincing recovery messages. That risk already reaches beyond email.

According to recent reports, unit 42 research tracked fake IT-support voice calls targeting over 150 employees across at least ten companies. The activity ran between January and April 2026.

Industry observers note that binance’s official risk account previously documented WhatsApp impersonators using supposed P2P account problems to solicit login QR-code scans. Ledger’s campaign tracker documented fake support calls and physical letters directing recipients toward recovery-phrase theft.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.

Recent findings suggest that after opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.

Industry observers note that the ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

Following the ID. Polo, the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

When the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Industry observers note that like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

Industry observers note that the ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen mentioned the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.

All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.

Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.

Volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.

Industry observers note that the base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

It has been revealed that volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

Recent findings suggest that in Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

It has been revealed that as the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”.

Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the upcoming ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

XRP has seen traders withdraw large amounts of tokens out of major crypto exchanges, especially Binance, over the last 30 days even as the broad market volatility persists.

Despite the intense selling pressure XRP has witnessed over the past few months, data from the crypto analytics platform Cryptoquant demonstrates that XRP’s exchange outflow has reached 5 billion XRP over the last month.

While the massive 30-day exchange outflow of 5 billion XRP is a relief signal because it signals persistent demand for XRP even amid the intense volatility, further data indicates that the outflow is relatively low compared to levels seen in October.

Although the 5 billion XRP outflow is significant and November has yet to wrap up, the data shows that it marks a decent decrease from October, when total exchange outflows for the month reached about 5.7 billion XRP.

Despite the 700,000 XRP decrease in the metric, the outflows registered in the last 30 days are still considered substantial and have drawn attention from market analysts as they signal strong investor conviction even as XRP suffered larger price losses this month compared with October.

Usually, increases in the exchange outflow of an asset suggest that investors are moving assets off exchanges into external wallets, most likely to hold them for longer periods.

Hence, this metric provides a bullish signal for XRP as it indicates strong demand among traders, putting Binance in the spotlight as over a billion XRP were withdrawn from the exchange during the period.

While OKX and Bybit saw traders withdraw 865.27 million XRP and 697.65 million XRP from their platforms, respectively, Binance registered the highest XRP withdrawals, with about 1.439 billion XRP leaving its exchange over the period.

#213483. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • According to recent reports, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • Recent findings suggest that just before 4 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

According to recent reports, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Recent findings suggest that just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

According to recent reports, then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson mentioned the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

In a recent development, it identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and states it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

Recent findings suggest that the report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

In a recent development, A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a massive truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

In a recent development, trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

It has been revealed that we want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a upcoming monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash reveals how late they can be.

In a recent development, our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

It has been revealed that three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

Recent findings suggest that that's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Recent findings suggest that either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck.
  • Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators claims Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

Sources indicate that the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

It has been revealed that according to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

Industry observers note that CHP states the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

According to recent reports, under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police stated it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Industry observers note that two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

Industry observers note that CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing latest rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

In a recent development, this is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

Recent findings suggest that the CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

According to recent reports, tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A tech giant that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

In a recent development, shiba Inu's (SHIB) market structure remains bearish. SHIB trades near $0.00000365 on November 26. Its daily chart is showing selling pressure, with no validated reversal. Therefore, realistic recovery scenarios are largely tied to a general market retracement rather than local developments.

Sources indicate that shiba Inu quite often follows general market trends, despite seeming like a memecoin leader. The illiquid market always creates certain concerns for assets like Shiba Inu. Apart from poor liquidity, another major factor is the lack of inflows into these assets.

Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, and other larger assets have been printing outflows throughout November. When larger assets do not attract enough capital, SHIB and smaller assets almost always witness outflows or passive positioning among investors.

#213479. How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2203 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay.
  • Industry observers note that over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture.
  • Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay. It’s an art form, a manipulation of material to achieve a desired end result that’s aesthetically appealing.

Industry observers note that over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture. We talk about sculpting one's back or legs, implying some kind of crafting of muscles, as if treating the human form like a sculpture. In fact, check the group class schedule of any gym these days, and you’ll likely spot the term “sculpt” appear somewhere on the lineup—directing toward some variation of a Pilates mat or strength training class, often involving lower weights and higher reps.

Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise? Is it a legitimate term or nothing more than strategic marketing language?

The exercise term actually dates back decades, with the first mentions appearing in fitness publications in the late 1970s. “It comes out of bodybuilding culture, which became more prominent in that period […] and you started to see the term ‘body sculpture,’” notes Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, a historian and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. And while there’s no clear record of who coined the term in a fitness context, there is speculation that it may have been inspired by German strongman Eugen Sandow (often called the "father of modern bodybuilding"), who referenced Greco-Roman sculptures as examples of the “ideal” physique in the late 19th century.

Recent findings suggest that in the 1980s, the idea of sculpting your muscles started to become much more mainstream, with the rise of aerobics, toning workouts, and fitness videos, indicates physical therapist and trainer Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, founder of Evlo Fitness. As instructors began using the term to describe and market workouts designed to shape and define specific muscles, “sculpting” became part of the everyday fitness vocabulary.

According to recent reports, the term also taps into something more personal: this idea that we have the power to change the shape of our own physiques. “I think that it really gained momentum because one, it kind of speaks to the artistry of the body or the artistry of fitness. Also, there's so much individual agency in this,” notes Petrezela. “It isn't about you just having the right genetics. Instead, you as an artist have the power to sculpt your own body.”.

Sources indicate that in the 1990s, however, the revered muscular look brought about by ’80s fitness culture made way for a celebration of thinner, more waifish bodies. “There was—and this is still the case—a lot of fear around getting too bulky,” states Petrezela. The term sculpting, however, molded into a promise of strength training without gaining too much muscle, which felt more palatable to women who feared such a physique.

“What's interesting is that we've changed the language over the years, but we're still selling women a very similar idea: that certain exercises will create a long, lean, toned appearance, while others will make them bulky,” says Ritchey.

In a recent development, if you worked out in the 2010s, you probably remember “sculpt” becoming a fixture of the boutique fitness boom. Still, while studio culture has waxed and waned over the last 20 years, the term has only gained traction, popping up across social media and on class schedules everywhere (think Pilates sculpt, yoga sculpt, and seemingly endless variations), notes Laura Girard, CPT, a NASM personal trainer and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Girard speculates that the popularity of sculpt classes may be buoyed by the widespread craving for more community in a post-pandemic world. After all, group fitness can be a fantastic third space. But there's another reason “sculpt” makes for such an appealing class name: It signals a particular kind of workout experience. Girard has observed “sculpt” used “almost like a dog whistle that [suggests] this class is going to be friendly for women and not scary, but still intense,” she says.

There's an aesthetic appeal, too. Petrezela believes the term’s resurgence of sorts has to do with how weightlifting and building muscle are very much having a moment, yet longstanding fears around getting “bulky” haven’t entirely disappeared. “It doesn't hurt that we are in a very, very image-driven moment in fitness culture,” she claims. “We're not just looking at the images in magazines that come out once a month, but our [social media] feeds are nonstop bodies all day—many of which are shared by influencers who have their own plans for how you can sculpt a body that looks just like theirs, or so they say.”.

It has been revealed that if you were to ask 10 different people on the street what a “sculpt class” is, you may get 10 different answers. To some, sculpt is synonymous with a mat Pilates routine, to others it might be a strength-training session, and to others it might be a yoga practice involving light dumbbells. So, can all of these workouts really fall under the same umbrella? And when a class promises to “sculpt,” is that an actual measurable result your muscles can deliver—or a feeling the name is designed to sell?

In a recent development, according to the experts, it’s largely the latter. “In a world where two things are popular—strength training and being very thin—’sculpting’ seems to be an appealing middle ground from a marketing perspective,” indicates Ritchey. “It promises ‘long, lean muscle tone’ without the perceived risk of building too much muscle.”.

She adds that “sculpt” is often used interchangeably with “toning,” which she describes as a “made-up term” that typically refers to changing your body composition (a.k.a., reducing fat and building muscle).

Because there's no single definition, what you actually do in a sculpt class can vary considerably. Still, Girard notes many sculpt classes share certain characteristics: lighter weights, choreography-inspired movements, and a lot of mat work. She also notes that while exercises are often fatiguing (think: that familiar muscle-burning sensation), they’re not necessarily pushing you to muscle failure via progressive overload (which is necessary for hypertrophy, or muscle-building).

According to recent reports, ritchey, who taught a sculpt class years ago, recalls using dumbbells and bodyweight for high reps. “We would do an entire three- to four-minute song of squats and lunges. That’s likely over 100 squats in a row, which burns and feels hard,” she says. Of course, it’s certainly possible to promote muscle-building with a low-weight, high-rep range, granted the programming is intentional. “But we know that if you could physically do more than about 30 reps in a row, the load is too light to build muscle.”.

Industry observers note that it’s important to note that a workout doesn't have to maximize muscle growth to be worthwhile. Certain sculpt classes can offer other benefits, from muscular endurance to simply providing motivation and enjoyment of exercising, often in a group setting. But if your primary goal is to significantly increase muscle size or change your body composition, not every sculpt class will provide the progressive resistance training needed to make that happen.

In a recent development, that’s where experts say the “sculpt” terminology can get confusing or misleading for some people. Girard fears that the language surrounding sculpt workouts reinforces misconceptions about women's bodies and what exercise can realistically change. “Sculpt as a verb is not a thing we can do to our bodies,” she notes. “We can gain or lose muscle. We can gain or lose fat, but that's more the role of nutrition. But we can't control how those muscles look.”.

In other words, there's no special exercise technique that creates “long, lean” muscles instead of so-called “bulky” ones. Your genetics influence your muscle shape, while your training can affect how much muscle you build. And the workout's name doesn't change those underlying principles.

According to recent reports, what’s more, at a time when there’s seemingly no consensus on how to talk about bodies or fitness in an empowering, nonoffensive way, Girard sees the term “sculpt” as potential coded language. While we may have mostly done away with, say, “bikini body shred” language in 2026, she fears that this nebulous term may be subliminally hinting at the same idea.

And while there's absolutely “nothing wrong with having aesthetic goals,” Ritchey stresses, “women deserve accurate information about how to achieve them.” If body recomp is their goal, they would have more success lifting close to failure and focusing on diet.”.

In a recent development, ultimately, your muscles don’t know whether you’re in a sculpt class or a traditional strength workout. Instead, they respond to the resistance, effort, and progression involved.

Industry observers note that “It’s funny because while all these trends come and go—and we will see sculpt come and go, too—the science never changes,” Ritchey says. “People just aren’t patient enough with the basics, so they jump on the latest trend thinking it will finally be the golden ticket to seeing results.”.

Because “sculpt” has no one definition, the quality, intensity, and overall experience of classes bearing the name can vary widely, too.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the workout itself, Girard points out that some sculpt classes can come with an unspoken expectation about who belongs in the room. As she’s observed: “These classes tend to be a self-selecting in-group. You may only see one type of body, or one specific outfit [...] That doesn’t mean it’s wrong or bad to be in a different outfit or in a different body, but it sure can feel that way.”.

According to recent reports, of course, there are also plenty of classes with “sculpt” in the name that are fantastic, inclusive workouts. This all boils down to the instructor, methods, and specific exercises they choose to incorporate—along with the type of community they cultivate. And, in many cases—particularly with larger studios or gyms—instructors have no say in what their class is actually called. “A lot of times, they're just doing what's trending to get people in the door,” states Girard.

Sources indicate that so if you’ve been curious to try a upcoming sculpt class at a local studio—by all means, go for it. Just be sure to go into it with eyes wide open, and give yourself permission to stop or pause or walk away if it doesn’t feel like a productive or positive environment for you. Pay attention to how the workout feels, how the instructor coaches, and whether the environment makes you feel welcome. One potential red flag? Aggressive “bikini body” messaging or marketing that frames building muscle as something to avoid. As Girard emphasizes, “It is definitely, definitely is not.”.

As the experts agree: Finding a form of movement you enjoy is the most important ingredient for establishing a healthy, consistent fitness routine. “My advice would be to ask yourself why you're doing these classes. Is it because you genuinely enjoy them? Or is it because you believe the burning sensation means you're toning and sculpting your muscles? Because those are two very different things,” indicates Ritchey.

In a recent development, have a sculpt workout you absolutely love? That’s wonderful, too. Finding movement you genuinely enjoy is one of the best ways to build a fitness routine you'll actually stick with. The important thing is understanding what you're getting out of it—and whether that aligns with what you're hoping to achieve.

“I want women to feel empowered to choose exercise based on what they enjoy and what actually works,” says Ritchey.

For someone primarily focused on building muscle, Ritchey recommends treating sculpt classes as opportunities for cardio or simply enjoyable movement, rather than as a replacement for progressive strength training.

They can even be great options for off days from lifting. “I don’t want to discourage anyone from moving,” she says. “But at the same time, we deserve to understand what is marketing and what our bodies actually respond to. We are all busy and tired and stressed [and] I want women to know how to best use their efforts to match their goals.”.

Recent findings suggest that appreciate the workout for what it is, understand what it isn't, and choose what works for you. That, in fact, is the true artistry of exercise.

Sources indicate that natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, is a professor of history at the Fresh School and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is a physical therapist, fitness instructor, and founder of Evlo Fitness. Laura Girard, CPT, is a NASM-certified personal trainer, founder of The Energy Academy, and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Kristine Thomason is a writer and editor with over a decade of experience creating content for print and digital publications. Previously, she was the health and fitness director at mindbodygreen, and the fitness and wellness editor at Women’s Health. Kristine's work has appeared in Men's Health, Travel + Leisure, Health, and Refinery29, among others. She holds a journalism degree from New York University, and is certified in personal training by the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in a recent turn of events, Fidelity Investments filed a Form S-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to launch a spot Chainlink [LINK] exchange-traded product (ETP).

Recent findings suggest that according to the 25th November filing, the proposed fund is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the provisional ticker FLNK. That said, the fund would also hold LINK tokens directly. This allows investors to gain exposure to LINK through traditional stock market accounts without having to purchase or manage the tokens themselves.

At the same time, the fund aims to track the Fidelity Chainlink Reference Rate, which calculates LINK’s price using a volume-weighted median methodology based on data from eligible spot markets.

Notably, its holdings would be managed by three proposed custodians, including Anchorage Digital Bank, BitGo Bank & Trust, and Coinbase Custody Trust Manufacturer.

According to recent reports, as expected, this news did have a positive impact on LINK’s price, which was trading at $9.16 at press time after a hike of 5.5% in the past 24 hours. With this, Fidelity becomes the third asset manager to launch a LINK ETF besides Grayscale’s GLNK and Bitwise’s CLNK.

In a recent development, in fact, according to SoSo Value data, GLNK and CLNK have already recorded cumulative net inflows of $128.12 million and $47.88 million, respectively. This in turn has brought their combined cumulative inflows to approximately $176 million. However, neither fund recorded any new flows on the 25th of November, with both showing $0 in daily net inflows.

It has been revealed that this news comes as the broader cryptocurrency investment products recorded widespread outflows across major digital assets in the month of November. Starting with Bitcoin [BTC] ETFs, which witnessed the largest withdrawals, worth approximately $5.39 billion in net outflows, facing their worst month since launch.

It has been revealed that ethereum [ETH] ETFs too saw $1.30 billion worth of outflows. This was followed by XRP ETFs, which saw $29.18 million in outflows, while Solana [SOL] ETFs registered withdrawals of $57 million. Meanwhile, Dogecoin [DOGE] ETFs recorded relatively smaller outflows of $409,130.

Industry observers note that interestingly, not all products experienced negative flows, as HBAR ETFs attracted approximately $1.71 million in net inflows. This made it the only asset in the sea of ETFs to record positive flows on the day.

The milestone is another sign of the community’s ongoing interest in Shiba Inu’s tokenomics as investors look for developments that could create stronger demand across the ecosystem.

The daily burn rate of Shiba Inu has seen a huge spike of 443%, as the SHIB community continues its attempt to shrink the circulating supply of the cryptocurrency.

A higher burn rate indicates more tokens have been destroyed than on the previous day. According to Shibburn, 4.40 million SHIB have been burned in the last 24 hours, with the daily burn rate jumping 443%. This contributes to a total of 8.42 million SHIB burned in the last seven days and 322.85 million SHIB sent to dead wallets in the last 30 days.

In a recent development, despite these cumulative burns, SHIB’s price performance still depends on broader market conditions and investor demand. At the time of writing, SHIB was up 5.60% in the last 24 hours to $0.00000364 amid the Thanksgiving holiday and down 6.45% weekly.

In the 22nd sanction packet, Russian-linked crypto services & platforms were specifically named as banned for transactions.

“The measures include the possibility for EU firms to sue their non-Russian contractual parties in the EU to recover damages.”, – states the document. “We will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia demonstrates genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine”, further said the Chief Commissioner.

With this package, we are increasing the pressure.We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms.We are further isolating Russia. We are shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events.… pic.twitter.com/9Ltkpohylq.

While focusing on Russian SWIFT sanctions, the EU added 51 entities to the anti-circumvention list, while the majority of them, 27, were outside Russia: 14 came from China, including four in Hong Kong, four in Türkiye, three in Kyrgyzstan, two in India, two in Kazakhstan and two more in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

In a recent development, the European Union (EU) freshly assembled the Crypto Task Force to counter fresh crypto-related ways of evading the huge pile of sanctions, including limitations of Russian business abroad via ‘third-world’ parties. The Council will decide when the ban enters into force, after the necessary measures are activated.

Tech Report: Ginger Rogers at Home: 10 Photos of the Golden Age Icon’s Glamorous SoCal Life

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home.
  • Recent findings suggest that decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the massive screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic.
  • Recent findings suggest that after Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home. “The little four-room house at 100 Moore Street was the perfect choice” for the future icon’s July 1911 welcome to the world, Rogers concluded in her 1991 memoir, Ginger: My Story. The star would go on to live with her extended family in Kansas City at 3306 Bellefountain Street; with her stepfather in Fort Worth at 1510 Cooper Street; and once she became a Hollywood sensation, a sprawling Beverly Hills estate. That joy and sense of peace she found in her childhood residence became a defining feature of her California pad. “It was a fun house, a happy house,” Rogers told Architectural Digest in 1994. “I was never angry when I didn’t have to work, because I liked to stay home so much.”.

Recent findings suggest that decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the massive screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic. Tom Holland will star as Astaire. Read on for a glimpse inside the Oscar winner’s off-set life in the places she cherished most.

Rogers on the diving board in 1938.

Recent findings suggest that after Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together. “I asked Mother if she would like me to build her a house, and if she did, could I live in it with her,” Rogers wrote in her memoir. “The next day she scoured the area for a suitable place to build. She found a wonderful lot high in Beverly Hills on 2.75 acres on Gilcrest Drive in Coldwater Canyon. It had a view that didn’t stop; when the fog burned off late every afternoon, it was possible to see Catalina.” Rogers is pictured at the stunning estate in this 1938 photo.

The actor with her home ice cream fountain.

According to recent reports, the Swing Time star added many personal touches to the home, one of which was an elaborate soda fountain. In this 1940 photo, she’s shown whipping up a sweet treat. In her memoir, Rogers recalled all the amenities she installed. “The building took over a year because of labor strikes and material shortages,” she wrote. “When the house was finished, it proved to have been worth waiting for. It had everything I wanted or needed in a house: swimming pool, tennis court, projection room, and my very own soda fountain. Who could ask for anything more?”.

Rogers opened her home tennis court to championship hopefuls so they could get practice matches in.

Recent findings suggest that rogers was an avid tennis player. Though she’s pictured here in 1950 at her Malibu beach house, the actor also had a home court installed at Gilcrest Drive. “On the way to the pool and tennis court were eight sculptured bay leaf trees. Next to the blue-tiled pool was my tennis court. This was my pride and joy,” she wrote in Ginger: My Story. With the knowledge that Rogers had the only en-tout-cas court in the area, the Tennis Association “begged” her to invite young hopefuls for some practice before they went on to championship matches at Forest Hills, Upcoming York. “I was delighted to open my court to competitors like Pancho Gonzales, Gussie Moran; and, later, Billie Jean King, Jennifer Hood, and Alice Marble slammed a few over the net too,” Rogers said.

Rogers was known for hosting her Hollywood star friends at home in Beverly Hills.

In a recent development, the Top Hat actor’s Beverly Hills abode was also a hot party spot for Rogers’s A-list friends. “My home was made for entertaining and I gave party after party,” she wrote in her memoir. “Most of them were informal. I’d serve spaghetti and we’d play some night tennis. Alcohol was never served, just cold drinks. One, a mixture of finely crushed ice, 7-Up, and concentrated orange juice, was a real favorite with the tennis crowd.”.

The star had a close relationship with her mother, Lela.

Rogers loved living with her mother, with whom she’s pictured in the circa 1940s portrait on the piano in this 1954 image. The triple threat pushed back against the term “stage mother” in Architectural Digest; she considered her mom to be “my guide and my professor… she was my encyclopedia. She knew what route to take: She helped Lucille Ball along hers too, you know. It would have been hard to have a career without her.” About their Beverly Hills pad, she added, “we both liked the look of a French farmhouse. And I wanted certain specific things: a helpful bath, a tennis court, and my own projection room, where we had eight or ten director’s chairs, so that friends could come over to watch movies.”.

Rogers with a furry friend at home in the 1950s.

In a recent development, the home featured a main house with bedrooms for Rogers and her mom, as well as a guesthouse for visitors. “The house was very bright,” she told Architectural Digest. “I don’t like dark things; even in my clothing, I prefer to be light and colorful—Springtime for Henry has always been my motto,” she explained, referencing the 1934 comedy. In her memoir, Rogers added, “The style was an American farmhouse with Dutch doors opening to cool breezes. The large bay window in the corner of the living room had a view of Beverly Hills and a bit of Los Angeles. Off the living room was a patio for barbecuing on a flagstone area under a beautiful Australian pepper tree. It was a wonderful place to entertain on crisp California nights.”.

Rogers’s home also included a solarium, and bedrooms with scenic views. “On a lower level was an outside entrance to the playroom,” the actor noted in her memoir. “This room had big windows and comfortable cushions as did the solarium in the hallway to the patio. I read many a book, with apple in hand, buried in those downy cushions.” About her bedrooms, she added, “There were two bedrooms leading from the solarium, one for Lelee [her mother] with a four-posted bed and one for me. My room looked out on the view of Beverly Hills, and I had a beautiful hand-carved mantel for my fireplace.”.

Rogers at work on an oil painting.

In addition to the stage talents for which she became a star, Rogers was also a painter. Her guesthouse also doubled as a studio. “My studio, which could double as a guesthouse, held all the paraphernalia of my hobbies: painting materials, canvases, paintbrushes, turpentine, pencils, and so on,” she wrote in her memoir. “Whenever there was a lull on set, I’d take out my pencil and sketch,” Rogers added. “I had been drawing for a long time and it seemed to come naturally to me. I found it challenging and relaxing. I never studied drawing or painting, I just did it.”.

In her memoir, Rogers recalled a time when she brought her paintings out for a gallery show. “When I’m not working or traveling, my main source of relaxation comes from my painting,” she wrote. “Gallery owners have wanted to have a one-person show of my work, but I never had the time to organize my paintings. Well, now was the time. Gregg Juarez, a gallery owner and friend of mine, arranged for a show and sale at his gallery in Palm Desert. As we were hanging the paintings for display, I realized these were my children—I couldn’t sell them! Gregg told me I had to sell a few so the customers wouldn’t get mad. I managed to put a few up for sale, but couldn’t part with the rest. So now they are joyously hung in my home for all to see.”.

Rogers was 83 years old when she died in 1995 at home in California.

It has been revealed that rogers remained at her home on Gilcrest Drive until 1970, when her mom urged her to sell while she was away working in Europe. “I had been renting it out more than living in it lately, and Mother thought it was financially sound to put it on the market,” the actor wrote in her memoir. “Besides, she said it needed a new roof! She handled all the details of the sale…. This was one time I’m not sure Mother knew best. I adored that house on Gilcrest Drive and have regretted selling it ever since.” Rogers died decades later, on April 25, 1995, at her home in Rancho Mirage, per the Los Angeles Times.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that when Jennifer Lawrence joined Instagram in September, fans rejoiced at the idea of seeing more content from the actress known for her sarcastic humor and likable authenticity.
  • In an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that when Jennifer Lawrence joined Instagram in September, fans rejoiced at the idea of seeing more content from the actress known for her sarcastic humor and likable authenticity. What we didn’t see coming was the launch of her newly introduced hair care brand Mes° Beauty (pronounced “mess”) and the public backlash that followed.

In an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public. “She saw the numbers Rihanna, Selena Gomez, and Hailey Bieber were pulling in, and suddenly decided to join Instagram, too. Not necessarily to connect with her audience, but perhaps to tap into the same commercial machine and sell us even more stuff,” wrote one Instagram commenter.

JLaw teamed up with Jasmina Aganovic, founder of biotech beauty organization Arcaea Labs, to formulate the brand’s hair care. As they say, the proof is in the pudding, so when I was sent all three products in a PR mailer, I knew I wanted to put them to the test.

Read my full, honest review of Mes° Beauty’s hair mask, serum, and volume mist below.

An intensive repair mask designed to be applied to dry hair anytime before washing. The milky-colored mask has a silky yet sticky, gelatin-like consistency that clings to your hair as you apply it. According to the brand, the mask prevents breakage and wash-day protein loss and protects the hair’s lipid barrier.

The Multitask Repair Mask differs from other hair masks because you apply it before shampooing and can leave it on for five minutes or overnight. With such a wide treatment time, it might take some trial and error to find the “sweet spot” for your hair type. During my testing, I applied a generous coat of the mask 5 to 10 minutes before shampooing. The second time, I tried applying a thinner coat of the mask, then pinned my hair up with a claw clip for about two hours before rinsing it out. The longer you wear it, the better the results. I would recommend applying a light coat before going about your day; that way, the scent isn’t overpowering and it won’t drip on your clothes.

After just two uses, my hair looked shinier and felt more hydrated after styling. As someone who rarely plans my hair care routine ahead of time, I appreciate that I can apply the mask just five minutes before I hop in the shower and still get noticeable results.

Although Mes° indicates the mask doubles as a styler for a glossy wet-hair look, I wouldn’t use it in that way. I think the product's consistency is too sticky and would be uncomfortable and messy (literally) to wear all day.

Some reviewers have mentioned a slightly off-putting smell. While the scent doesn’t bother me (it smells like a light, musky fragrance), it may not be for everyone. If I’m paying $52 for a hair mask, it would be nice to have a luxurious fragrance to add to the experience. If a brand is going to do musk, really lean into it with notes of sandalwood, amber, or patchouli.

It has been revealed that the packaging also makes the product difficult to use. In the mailer I received, the mask comes in a GoGo Squeez-like pouch that you’re supposed to empty into the plastic tub. However, dipping my fingers into the tub felt clumsy, and next time I would just dispense directly from the pouch.

A bi-phase serum that smooths frizz, restores shine, and provides heat protection up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit. The “bi-phase” claim comes from combining a lightweight oil and a serum in the formula. After touching it, applying it, and letting it sit in my hair for a few days, I think calling it a serum is misleading. The consistency and the way it applies are much more like a hair oil.

On day two hair, I warmed two drops of the Off-Duty Restyling Serum between my palms, and worked it through my strands. I have very thick, straight, shoulder-length hair, so when I applied the serum up through my mid-lengths, it was way too oily. I don’t know if I would use it to restyle my hair unless I was planning to use a hot tool.

Recent findings suggest that I also tested the serum as a finishing product, applying it to my ends after blow-drying. I found this to be the most effective way to use the product on my hair type.

Industry observers note that overall, the Off-Duty Restyling Serum doesn’t make much sense to me. What’s the point of having heat protection if it’s made for “reshaping yesterday’s style?” Are we going back in with more heat? To me, that sounds like an extra step in my morning routine that I do not have the time or patience for.

On days when I wash and blow-dry my hair, I like using a tiny amount of the serum just on my ends, and I've found it dries down nicely and leaves my hair soft and touchable. That stated, I own other lightweight hair oils that work just as well for a fraction of the price—like FromLabs’ Protein Capsule Hair Repair Oil. If you have fine, wavy, or curly hair, the Off-Duty Serum may work better for you.

A lightweight spray that reduces scalp oiliness for lasting lift. Instead of creating gritty texture or absorbing excess oil like a dry shampoo, the Good Roots mist helps balance the scalp microbiome to produce less oil at the roots, extending the time until your next wash.

Over the past two weeks, I tested the Good Roots mist in three ways: applying it to damp hair before blow-drying, applying it to damp hair before air-drying, and applying it to dry day-two and day-three hair.

After about five uses of trial and error, I found it worked best when I applied it to my clean, damp roots and blow-dried. The heat felt like it helped dry down and “activate” the mist, whereas letting my hair air-dry didn’t produce much volume.

Industry observers note that pro-Tip: Be sure to hold the bottle about a foot away for even misting. The applicator pump doesn’t produce a fine spritz, and it took me a few uses to get that right.

According to recent reports, after two weeks of testing, the Good Roots Volume Mist is my favorite of the trio. Two key ingredients, the proprietary Arc-5 Technology and the Mediterranean microalgae, help support a balanced scalp, keeping your hair fresher longer. With consistent use, the Good Roots mist extended my time between hair washes—I typically wash every other day, but I was able to go a third day. Plus, the Juniperus virginiana oil in the formula has a fresh, woody scent that reminds me of a fancy sea salt spray.

It has been revealed that I also like that the mist doesn’t make my hair feel super gritty or textured the way a dry shampoo might. That said, I have other dry shampoo products that do a lot more heavy lifting than this volume mist. If I’m looking to achieve noticeable volume and lift in my thick hair, the Good Roots mist doesn’t cut it.

It has been revealed that my general critique of Mes° Beauty is that the products are not very intuitive. They seem straightforward, but the brand doesn’t give great direction on how to get the most out of them. After the first one or two uses, you may feel they barely do anything at all. But if you learn how to use them properly when styling your hair, they can perform fairly well.

Mes° is supposed to be about “Less time fixing your hair. More time living,” but in reality, achieving that effortlessly chic, tousled look requires a fair bit of effort. In my opinion, this lineup is much more suited to someone who blows out or flat irons or curls their hair once or twice a week and wants to extend their style. For my hair type, these products don’t fit into my routine in a way that makes sense, but if you have fine and/or wavy hair, they might work better for you.

Sources indicate that curious about my other hair standbys? They’re right now $30 and under—and make for excellent beauty gift ideas for your loved ones for the upcoming holiday season.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holding a basket of different tokens often feels like diversification, right up until a market downturn drags them all down at once.
  • Toobit’s chief growth officer, Yasser Elmansy, told CryptoSlate he’d like an AI assistant to warn traders when a new position adds to a risk they already carry.
  • For Elmansy, the goal isn’t to hand trading over to bots, but to give retail users better visibility before they click buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holding a basket of different tokens often feels like diversification, right up until a market downturn drags them all down at once.

Toobit’s chief growth officer, Yasser Elmansy, told CryptoSlate he’d like an AI assistant to warn traders when a new position adds to a risk they already carry.

For Elmansy, the goal isn’t to hand trading over to bots, but to give retail users better visibility before they click buy.

Trading once required a phone call to a broker; the internet moved it to computers, and smartphones put market access in people’s pockets.

“The internet changed how we execute decisions; AI could change how we prepare for and make them,” he says.

In a recent development, elmansy imagines an assistant that, with a trader’s permission, could review holdings, open positions, leverage, and trading history. Suppose the trader owns several tokens that tend to move together. The assistant could explain how a single downturn might affect all those positions and how leverage can magnify a loss.

The trader would still set objectives and risk limits, authorize access, and approve consequential actions.

“I’d rather see AI help someone make a better-informed decision than simply push them to trade more.”.

In a recent development, models can misread information or produce convincing but wrong explanations, he warns, and in a leveraged market, small errors can be costly. If many automated strategies react to the same signals, they can worsen volatility.

“Speed isn’t always an advantage if everyone responds in the same way,” he claims.

He wants leverage controls and clear ways to pause or stop automation.

It has been revealed that that emphasis on informed participation carries over into how Elmansy approaches growth at Toobit. He helps choose partners among trading communities and creators and discusses deal terms. Rather than chasing raw follower counts, he looks at how many people actively trade, how long they stay involved, and how much trading takes place.

He says Toobit already uses those criteria to assess prospective partners.

“I don’t want to attach a specific growth figure to that work without verified reporting,” he says.

The chief growth officer role is recent, he indicates, so he “wouldn’t claim to have transformed the business in that capacity already.” What has changed is the scope of his thinking.

“To me, sustainable growth isn’t only about why owners arrive; it’s also about why they stay,” he adds.

Elmansy’s focus on building durable systems and questioning standard playbooks comes from two decades of learning business and crypto from the ground up.

His first venture started in sixth grade, when he told his brother and a relative he was working in advertising and both asked to join.

“Rather than admitting I didn’t actually have a business, I decided to give them an assignment,” he says.

Armed with a print catalog from a shop his father’s accounting firm used, Elmansy learned that 100 business cards cost about three pounds to produce. He sent his recruits to nearby businesses, including a supermarket, to sell them for 20 pounds.

“To my complete surprise, they both came back with customers and money,” he recalls.

He placed the orders, delivered the cards, and started again. Websites and Facebook ads followed. For years he found the clients and did the work himself, until the business hit a wall because he couldn't scale alone. He convinced a backer to help fund an office and staff, and rolled out his first marketing agency in 2013, concluding that growth eventually requires trusting people and building structure.

Recent findings suggest that he remembers keeping pictures of Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg on that first office wall. He wanted to build his own technology company.

“I wasn’t interested in technology simply as a tool for marketing,” he indicates.

It has been revealed that by 2019, the agency had around 40 employees. When the pandemic hit, businesses cut marketing budgets, so he scaled back and spent late 2020 studying decentralized exchanges and liquidity pools.

After watching an OKX webinar, he contacted the exchange’s recruitment team. He lacked the business development background it wanted, but pitched his marketing and DeFi knowledge and got a chance.

When he joined, his manager mentioned a trading-volume target of $100,000.

“I genuinely didn’t know whether that was large or small,” he indicates.

In a recent development, what Elmansy did know was influencer marketing. At OKX, he indicates, he challenged assumptions about what the exchange should pay its partners and argued for backing deals he believed in. He spent nearly three and a half years at OKX, then worked at Pionex, before he joined Toobit in January 2026 as head of global business development.

Sources indicate that looking ahead, Elmansy thinks crypto will reach more people when sending money gets simpler. Today, he says, consumers still have to think about wallets, private keys, networks, and fees “before they can do something as basic as moving value.” He wants users to understand the risks they take even as the mechanics get easier.

Disclosure: This is a sponsored interview, paid for by Toobit. CryptoSlate interviewed Yasser Elmansy, Toobit’s chief growth officer, and all quotes come from that interview. This article is not investment advice. Crypto trading, especially with leverage, carries a risk of loss.
