Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one.
  • Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a new production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

If you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we announced a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the latest production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla plans to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company indicates it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

Sources indicate that it leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the newly introduced hall will be bigger than the original factory.

In a recent development, the building isn’t new. Tesla laid out a plan to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

Recent findings suggest that the EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Recent findings suggest that rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

According to recent reports, tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

Sources indicate that the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU mentioned no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

According to recent reports, and the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

It has been revealed that this is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI assistants can complete complex office tasks correctly while making recommendations that expose users to financial and operational risks.
  • According to recent reports, A newly introduced benchmark called ShellBench, released on Nov.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI assistants can complete complex office tasks correctly while making recommendations that expose users to financial and operational risks.

According to recent reports, A newly introduced benchmark called ShellBench, released on Nov. 24 by researchers from the OpenClaw Foundation and other organizations, found that 2,589 of the 26,151 runs that satisfied every correctness criterion failed at least one safety check.

That represents a 9.9% safety failure rate among otherwise successful runs, exposing a gap between AI agents' ability to complete assignments and their reliability when handling sensitive responsibilities.

The researchers evaluated 12 AI models across five agent harnesses, the software connecting models to external tools and files, generating 53,100 runs across 100 everyday tasks.

Follow the runs that met every correctness criterion to see how often they still failed on safety.

ShellBench graded correctness and safety separately.

In a recent development, the figures describe rule compliance under ShellBench’s Nov. 24 test design. The severity of real-world harm lies outside the study’s scope.

According to recent reports, the upper bar highlights 26,151 of 53,100 graded runs (49.25% by width). The lower bar expands that group and highlights 2,589 of 26,151 (9.9%, rounded to one decimal). Both bars use the counts reported by ShellBench.

Sources indicate that the figures describe rule compliance under ShellBench’s Nov. 24 test design. The severity of real-world harm lies outside the study’s scope.

The simulated workspaces contained documents, emails, and spreadsheets, including conflicting information and outdated records that assistants had to navigate to complete their assignments.

Across all evaluated runs, 8,340 (15.7%) failed at least one safety requirement.

The risks were particularly apparent in a freight invoice reconciliation task, where researchers evaluated whether AI assistants could determine appropriate payments from business records.

According to the research paper, 214 of 531 submissions (40.3%) failed a safety requirement governing payment recommendations.

The failures included recommendations to pay invoices twice, use inflated or incorrect payment amounts, and settle charges outside the appropriate billing period.

Such errors could become expensive as businesses give AI agents greater autonomy over accounting, procurement, and payment processing.

The risks also extend beyond financial transactions. In a separate planning exercise, failing to arrange a child's school pickup was sufficient to trigger a safety failure.

ShellBench's findings raise questions about whether businesses can rely on conventional accuracy and task completion metrics when deciding how much operational responsibility to delegate to AI agents.

Detecting these failures also presents challenges. Researchers used an AI judge to evaluate 90 of the benchmark's 100 tasks, with automated code tests grading the remainder.

The AI judge agreed with human reference labels in 89.9% of 278 individual grading decisions. In a separate reliability test, six of 40 unchanged submissions received conflicting pass and fail verdicts across repeated evaluations.

That inconsistency complicates efforts to automate oversight of AI systems performing sensitive work.

It has been revealed that while ShellBench measured simulated mistakes rather than actual financial losses, its findings expose a consequential vulnerability in autonomous AI deployment. An assistant can satisfy every requirement used to establish task correctness and still violate safeguards intended to protect the people delegating that work.

For businesses expanding AI agents' authority from preparing documents to executing transactions, that distinction could determine whether an otherwise successful assignment becomes a financial liability.

KuCoin will delist Monero (XMR) on Nov. 30, the exchange revealed on Thursday. XMR dropped as low as $436 after the announcement and lost almost 15% within four hours, according to Kraken data on TradingView.

In the notice, KuCoin said that XMR would be delisted "in accordance with the Special Treatment Rules of KuCoin." The exchange closed XMR deposits on Thursday and will remove the XMR/USDT, XMR/USDC, XMR/ETH and XMR/BTC pairs at 08:00 UTC on Nov. 30.

Industry observers note that kuCoin will also shut down XMR trading bots, Convert swaps and Earn products before the delisting. Owners can withdraw XMR until Dec. 31, and KuCoin said that it could close withdrawals earlier if the Monero network stops producing blocks or processing transfers.

On Thursday, KuCoin's XMR/USDT pair had $73.8 million in 24-hour volume, according to CoinMarketCap. It was the largest Monero spot market and accounted for 47% of XMR spot trading. HTX's XMR/USDT pair was second with $29.5 million.

According to recent reports, kuCoin did not mention its XMRUSDT perpetual contract in the notice. The contract had $33 million in 24-hour volume on Thursday, according to CoinMarketCap. Binance had the largest XMR perpetual market with $89.3 million.

It has been revealed that perpetualCow, who promotes the Wagyu trading platform on X, also responded to the delisting. "Over 50% of people sourced their XMR indirectly from KuCoin; it fuelled ALL instant swap exchanges," he wrote on Thursday. According to PerpetualCow, instant swap services "don't have their own liquidity" and "simply wrapped around KuCoin and sold/bought into their order books.".

In the same post, he wrote that Wagyu had done more than $1.5 billion in volume in less than a year. He also shared a screenshot of Wagyu's XMR-USDC market together with the post, and it showed $63.5 million in 24-hour volume.

Recent findings suggest that earlier in November, the MEXC exchange also delisted XMR. The exchange removed XMR spot and perpetual markets on Nov. 13.

Recent findings suggest that OKX delisted XMR in January 2024, and Binance removed the coin on Feb. 20, 2024. Binance remarked at the time that it would conduct a deeper review "when a coin or token no longer meets this standard, or the industry changes." XMR fell more than 15% after the Binance announcement.

Sources indicate that kraken stopped XMR trading for clients in the European Economic Area at the end of October 2024. In August 2025, Kraken revealed an XMR delisting for Canadian clients "due to recent compliance requirements in Canada" and disabled trading for them on Sept. 2, 2025.

  • SLING BAGS ARE here to stay, gentlemen, and to be honest, they’re a lighter and smarter way to commute with your EDC when backpacks and duffel bags feel like overkill.

  • Industry observers note that we gave 20 different sling bags a test run, but Lululemon’s offering takes the cake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SLING BAGS ARE here to stay, gentlemen, and to be honest, they’re a lighter and smarter way to commute with your EDC when backpacks and duffel bags feel like overkill. Worn across the body (unlike a fanny pack, which is designed to sit around the waist), sling bags are easy to carry, super practical, and able to transport all your daily essentials using a bunch of accessible compartments, zippers, and pockets. The best sling bags for men offer a range of styles for every kind of guy, whether you’re commuting, traveling, or heading into the outdoors. Some are minimal and sleek, while others favor the rugged and technical.

If you’re stuck on which sling bag to pick, don’t sweat it—our team tested and narrowed down the top contenders. Below, we’ve included 11 standout picks that combine comfort, style, and hands-free functionality from notable brands like Peak Design, Lululemon, and The North Face.

Industry observers note that we gave 20 different sling bags a test run, but Lululemon’s offering takes the cake. The Everywhere Belt Bag is all about making things easier for the man on the go. For starters, you can throw it over your shoulder or wear it around your waist like a fanny pack for when you're on the trail or at an outdoor concert (or any other time you want to be hands-free). The main pouch features a double two-way zipper that opens three-quarters of the way, letting you see and reach everything inside without having to dig around blindly. Another bonus: There’s a smaller pocket tucked into the back with a single zipper, which makes it ideal for hiding cash, cards, and other small valuables.

Sources indicate that thanks to the water-resistant nylon exterior, anything stowed away will remain dry, in the event it starts pouring rain. Our favorite part, however, is the strap that we found to be one of the most comfortable ones that we’ve tested. As for the colorway, you can choose from a bunch of neutral tones, but our fashion team recommends going with the eucalyptus hue—you’re bound to be the center of attention.

Sources indicate that while it can’t store a water bottle, we love how effortlessly our gadgets and snacks fit inside. Not to mention, it has so much versatility in regard to style. You can wear it with your best sweatsuit or casual fit and look fly for the day’s festivities.

Read More: Best Fanny Packs for Men.

Recent findings suggest that this Amazon best-seller is spot-on for your next adventure. It’s really got organization in spades with mesh pockets on two sides for bottles or umbrellas, a small front zipper pocket for smaller devices, and a significant space inside that’s designed like a backpack. It’s smartly compartmentalized into smaller sections for anything from keys, passports, snacks, and other bits and bobs. During a camping trip, we made use of the main pocket inside, which is big enough to store your phone and tablet, a feature that we deemed essential in a travel sling bag.

In a recent development, you can even enjoy your music on your commute as the convenient opening on the front provides easy access to your earphones. It comes in every color imaginable, but the teal blue and reflective details will help you stand out and offer nighttime visibility. And unlike others in this guide, this one comes with a water bottle holder, so you stay hydrated on the move.

Read More: Best Backpacks for Men.

As one of the smaller sling bags in our guide, the Topo Designs Mini Quick Pack has substantial storage where it matters most. We found that its capacity is perfect for shorter trips and daily errands, and the straps are a piece of cake to adjust (though there are quite a few straps). Whenever we don’t need a huge backpack and want to pack light, this little guy is a star.

It has been revealed that in our experience, we’ve worn it on the waist and across the body. One tester was able to utilize the bike light attachment loop for a nighttime ride to increase visibility. And with a solid amount of space and interior organization for a phone, cardholder, and other odds and ends, our editors have also tucked it under a thin coat when we’re in a tight spot. Plus, the unique color-blocked design earns it some extra style points.

According to recent reports, while we still feel it works great for the city, this ruggedly built sling is perfect for outdoor adventurists. Firstly, it’s offered in two different sizes with a 6- or 9-liter size, ensuring that if you need a little extra space, you can spend an extra $10 to upgrade. Even in the smaller size, you can easily fit a water bottle plus all of your other gear like earbuds, sunglasses, phone, EDC essentials, protein bar, plus more thanks to the expandable gusset.

Sources indicate that one of the cool features of this bag that you won’t find on others is that it comes with sturdy quick-release buckles on both sides, making it ideal no matter which shoulder you toss it around. It offers various storage compartments, 10 to be exact, even with a soft-lined pouch that is great for your phone or sunglasses, helping to avoid scratching while on the move—plus, the padded back and bottom help to protect everything else. Its water resistance and six-year warranty make it the perfect outdoor bag.

Recent findings suggest that the North Face’s Base Camp Voyager Sling is basically a mini backpack in disguise that’s built to take a beating. This thing held up through packed subways, bike rides, and overhead bin shoves without a single scuff. The shell’s made from abrasion-resistant polyester fabric, the same ultra-tough material as the brand’s duffels, which are designed for actual expeditions, so your daily commute? No sweat.

Industry observers note that there’s a padded sleeve that snugly fits a tablet, reflective accents for low-light visibility (great for late-night rides), and a thick, padded shoulder strap that’s actually comfortable to wear all day. Bonus: There’s a zip pocket on the strap that perfectly fits your phone, so no more digging around at crosswalks.

Recent findings suggest that we also loved how the design leans more toward a backpack than a bag. It’s minimalist, structured, and doesn’t flop around when you’re on the move. Whether you’re weaving through downtown foot traffic or navigating an airport terminal, this is the kind of sling that keeps up, and doesn’t look out of place when you stop for a coffee.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a more elevated sling, then you’ll definitely want to grab this leather Blake Belt Bag from Leatherology. We recommend opting for the standard-size model, as it holds about 5 liters, but it also comes in slim and mini models. You can choose from 10 colors, including three in smooth full-grain, six in pebbled full-grain, a black croc leather, and a groovy fairway green color (very reminiscent of The Masters’ signature color).

It has been revealed that the adjustable strap is quite versatile, with the options of wearing it as a traditional crossbody bag, hanging off one shoulder, or around the waist, though, as it’s a unisex model, the strap may be just a touch too short for some guys. That noted, it can hold a good amount of gear with its main zippered compartment, which comes with four interior card slots and a decent-sized interior mesh pocket that is also zippered. While some note that the zippers are a little stiff, over time they do tend to wear in and work much easier. Plus, for an additional fee, you can personalize it to truly make it one of a kind.

It has been revealed that eddie Bauer’s Mini Crossbody Bag proves that you don’t have to spend substantial to get a reliable everyday carry. Made from nylon, this compact bag punches above its weight when it comes to utility. During testing, we found the slightly 0.8L capacity to be just right. It’s big enough to fit your phone, wallet, keys, and a lip balm, but small enough to stay light and nimble when you’re clocking your daily step count goal. I love the front cargo pocket that has a flap closure. It kept essentials like subway cards or AirPods secure but easy to access when we were on the go.

Yeah, it’s too small to carry a tablet or water bottle, but it comes in clutch for light carry days and quick errands. One tester wore it on a weekend trip and appreciated how easy it was to sling over a jacket without ever feeling bulky. The strap adjusts smoothly and stays comfortable during hours of walking, and after a few days of use, the bag still looked good as latest.

Reigning Champ’s crossbody bag is reliable for outdoor gear because it combines smart construction and water-resistant materials. This resilient twill bag is the practical choice to go anywhere, and though it may look compact, there’s plenty of space and interior pockets to keep your stuff organized without looking overloaded. I even wore this during a rainy evening commute, and everything inside, from my phone to loose bills, stayed bone dry.

According to recent reports, the adjustable webbing strap is quite comfortable, even if you proposal on wearing it all day long. With it, you get two main zippered pockets, plus an internal zippered pocket, and you even get a small front-facing zippered pocket for quick access when you need it. Though it only comes in one color, there’s really not a more versatile accessory color than black, anyway. And it looks darn good with a slight pop of white in its logo.

We love a bag that comes in more than one size, and the Everyday Sling from Peak Design comes in three different sizes: 3-, 6-, and 10-liter options, making it one of the most versatile choices available. Not only that, but it’s also available in seven different colors, ensuring that whatever your taste is, there is definitely a pick for you. Another thing that we really like about this bag is the ability to loosen (or tighten) the quick-adjuster and padded straps while still wearing it.

While this bag is designed with creatives in mind to be able to hold all of your tech, like cameras, laptops (depending on size choice), lenses, rangefinders, and more (thanks to its comfy and padded design), it can still be a great option to use hiking or biking with its weatherproof design and 400D shell construction. While it is resistant to the elements, some reviewers do mention to be cautious with heavier rainfall, though the majority note it can handle most situations.

According to recent reports, traveling around the city, either to and from work, running errands, or just heading to the local coffee shop means finding a bag that’s just substantial enough to hold the essentials, yet one that’s not gonna weigh you down. Aer’s City Sling 2 is the perfectly sized bag for city activities and commuting. It weighs under a pound and holds 2.5 liters, which means you can still get all of your EDC gear in there with ease.

According to recent reports, even though it’s lightweight, it’s darn tough with its 700D Cordura nylon design and aircraft-grade aluminum tension locks, which means you don’t sacrifice durability. It has a quick-access front pocket for things like keychains, while its back zippered pocket is better for valuables like passports or wallets, with ample room in its main zippered compartment, too. Plus, its strap hides away thanks to its magnetic fastener, converting it into a mobile dopp kit in a pinch. While the strap is tough, it may be a little rough on the shoulder after a day of wear.

Oakley’s Extractor Sling is basically a backpack in disguise, making it perfect for work commutes. It has the capacity to serve as one with several compartments and pockets to transport goods like your hand cream, portable charger, and office laptop. We found this sling bag specifically useful for when we want to pack more without overdoing it.

You can even fit your gym shorts and workout shirts inside to hit a quick session once you’re off the clock. Plus, the back panel is equipped with air channels to help deliver more breathability and comfort while you’re on the move. Although the downside is that it is heavier than others we’ve tested, it’s got the volume you need to load it all in.

Recent findings suggest that the best sling bags for men should offer features that cater to your needs. Typically smaller than a messenger bag, they can be worn across the body, over a shoulder, or even around the waist. The sling bags in our guide range from 1.5 liters of capacity to 30 liters.

Recent findings suggest that when looking for one, consider the layout and accessibility of the compartments, pockets, and dedicated spaces for laptops, smartphones, tablets, or water bottles. All in all, there should be ample storage capacity (usually measured and listed in liters) that allows for smart organization and easy reach.

In a recent development, since sling bags are often worn over one shoulder or across the body, the best sling bags for men need to have adjustable straps and padding to distribute weight evenly across your shoulders and back—a properly fitted sling bag should feel comfortable and not strain you even when worn for extended periods. Therefore, pay attention to the strap’s material, width, and adjustability.

Sources indicate that A lightweight sling bag is usually better since it is easier to carry and feels better on your body by preventing unnecessary strain on your shoulders and back, especially if you plan to use the sling bag for hours on end, or carry it while hiking. Ultimately, the weight of a sling bag will depend on the bag's capacity, design, and intended uses.

To find the best sling bags for men, myself and Joseph Cheatham, led by our Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower, put them through real-life situations. We loaded them up with our usual gear like our phone, wallet, keys, snacks, even a water bottle to see how they handle the weight. The ones we tested have been worn at outdoor festivals, during day hikes, through long-haul flights, and of course, out and about running weekend errands. We paid close attention to the pockets and zippers, but really made sure to assess how comfortable the adjustable straps lie on our shoulders.

Industry observers note that many sling bags are actually designed to accommodate laptops or tablets. These sling bags usually fall on the larger, more functional side, with a large capacity and spacious interior compartment, as well as dedicated padded compartments or sleeves that offer protection and secure storage for your electronic devices.

Sling bags are versatile just like backpacks, hence, with the right style and design, they can work in a variety of places. A sleek, leather option looks professional enough for the office and goes well with your office fits. A rugged, weather-resistant one is great for outdoor activities—in fact, there are sling bags designed for purposes like hiking and traveling. For your casual outings, a small, stylish sling bag will work wonders.

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. In a recent development, solana is four days away from matching a record last seen in 2022. SOL has lost 25.7% in November so far (as of Nov. 26). That's likely to become the cryptocurrency's ninth losing month this year. If December also ends in the red, that would bring the total to 10, the highest number of losing months in a single year in SOL's history.

In terms of percentage losses, 2022 was overwhelmingly the worst year for Solana. SOL lost 94.15% in 2022. So far in 2026, it's down 43.09%.

SOL declined every month between January and July. August brought a 41.5% surge, followed by another 14.56% gain in September. Then, October and November erased all those gains.

As of Nov. 26, Bitcoin had fallen roughly 21% in November. That provides some context. In October, BTC dropped 7.32%, while SOL lost 19%. Solana was already underperforming Bitcoin before November's losses accelerated.

Meanwhile, another source of demand is faltering. U.S. spot Solana ETFs have recorded $164 million in net outflows over the 30 trading days leading up to Nov. 25.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 6, investors withdrew about $24 million from these funds. By Nov. 25, when SOL was trading around $70, the funds recorded zero net inflows. Lower prices had not yet brought ETF investors back in significant numbers.

Solana's network activity actually grew during the summer rally. Quarterly trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) increased 23% from the previous quarter to $197 billion in Q3.

Industry observers note that of that, a record $7.1 billion came from tokenized equities. That's roughly 3.6% of the quarter's total volume.

Much of the third-quarter growth came from memecoins, according to Bitwise. On Nov. 26, the memecoin platform Pump accounted for $1.29 million of the $2.69 million in daily protocol revenue on Solana tracked by DefiLlama.

Industry observers note that for SOL to recover and break even in November, it would need to rise about 34.6% by Nov. 30.

If November ends in the red, even a small decline in December would give Solana a record 10th losing month of the year.

According to recent reports, december ended lower in five of the last six years shown on the chart. However, six data points aren't much to base a forecast on.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

It has been revealed that the Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

In a recent development, in China, the latest Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

According to recent reports, the second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s fresh Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the new version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

It has been revealed that with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

It has been revealed that even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

In a recent development, inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The latest setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

The optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

In China, BYD offers the newly introduced Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

It has been revealed that the current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the flagship cryptocurrency fell to $57,210 on Wednesday before recovering to close at $60,368, according to CryptoSlate's data.
  • However, the recovery comes as Bank of Japan officials signal that further monetary tightening may be necessary to contain inflation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin's recovery above $60,000 faces a fresh test from Japan's inflation report while US spot Bitcoin ETFs remain closed for Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that the flagship cryptocurrency fell to $57,210 on Wednesday before recovering to close at $60,368, according to CryptoSlate's data. Bitcoin extended those gains modestly on Thursday, trading around $60,538 as of 10:40 UTC.

However, the recovery comes as Bank of Japan officials signal that further monetary tightening may be necessary to contain inflation.

Speaking in Yamanashi on Thursday, BOJ board member Naoki Tamura said the central bank could accelerate interest rate increases if underlying inflation indicates signs of exceeding its 2% target.

Tamura also reaffirmed his estimate that Japan's neutral interest rate, the level at which monetary policy neither stimulates nor restrains economic activity, stands at around 2%. That is 75 basis points above the BOJ's current overnight policy rate of 1.25%, which the central bank maintained at its October meeting.

The yen strengthened modestly on Thursday, with BOJ data showing the dollar trading around 159.17 yen at 5 p.m. in Tokyo, compared with 159.21 earlier in the day.

Recent findings suggest that markets will get a fresh read on Japan's inflation trajectory when Tokyo publishes its preliminary November consumer price figures at 8:30 a.m. local time on Friday, equivalent to 6:30 p.m. ET on Thanksgiving.

The release precedes Japan's nationwide inflation report on Dec. 18, giving investors an earlier opportunity to reassess expectations for BOJ monetary policy.

That timing leaves Bitcoin exposed to changes in those expectations before US spot ETFs resume trading during Friday's shortened NYSE Arca session.

Japan's monetary tightening poses two distinct risks to investors who borrowed yen to finance positions in Bitcoin and other dollar-denominated assets.

The strategy, commonly known as the yen carry trade, involves borrowing in Japan's relatively low-interest-rate currency and deploying the proceeds into assets elsewhere in pursuit of higher returns.

A strengthening yen increases the dollar cost of repaying that debt for investors who have not hedged their currency exposure, eroding returns even when Bitcoin's price remains unchanged.

Higher Japanese interest rates compound that pressure by potentially increasing the cost of refinancing existing positions.

Together, those developments can make leveraged investments less profitable, encouraging traders to reduce exposure to risk assets to repay their yen-denominated liabilities.

The cost of a yen-funded position can rise even if Bitcoin’s dollar price holds steady.

Currency and refinancing costs can rise separately or together.

Actual costs depend on the loan and currency hedge.

The diagram separates the exchange-rate exposure of fixed yen principal from the interest expense of a replacement loan, following the BIS description of yen-funded carry.

Actual costs depend on the loan and currency hedge.

Sources indicate that japan's two-year government bond yield provides another indication of how investors are pricing the country's monetary policy outlook. A rise in short-term yields alongside a strengthening yen following Friday's inflation report would signal mounting pressure on yen-funded positions.

Conversely, softer inflation could temper expectations of accelerated BOJ tightening, easing one potential source of selling pressure on Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is that a hotter inflation reading could renew pressure on Bitcoin's fragile recovery while US spot ETF trading remains suspended. Those funds will reopen at 9:30 a.m. ET on Friday, approximately 15 hours after Tokyo's inflation release, leaving Bitcoin's continuously operating global markets to absorb the initial reaction.

A good run is supposed to lift your mood, not bring you down, so finding the best running shorts to keep the endorphins flowing (and your butt dry) is essential.

In a recent development, not all workout shorts are made the same. Some offer more compression, while others are less restrictive and have convenient features like pockets—the holy grail! “You need a place to carry all your resources—pockets are a non-negotiable for running gels, electrolytes, phone, wallet, and keys,” says Newly introduced York-based running coach and personal trainer Amanda Katz, NASM-CPT.

While many athletic shorts can be used for different purposes, running shorts usually have a built-in interior liner, sweat-wicking material, and a nonconstrictive design to keep you cool and comfortable as you rack up mileage in your sleek running shoes.

I researched and gathered the best running shorts from a running coach and editors who’ve personally tested them. Whether you’re training for a marathon or are a hobby jogger, all the shorts I picked are from trusted activewear and athleisure brands that will benefit you in the long run (literally). Ready to find out more about the best running shorts for women? Keep scrolling.

In a recent development, after testing countless pairs of running shorts over the years, the Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short from Lululemon is my fave for its sweat-wicking fabric and comfortable fit. The polyester blend wicks away sweat, prevents cling, and promotes airflow while running. The loose, flowy fit keeps me cool, while a built-in interior liner adds lightweight coverage and support without bulk.

The side pockets are small, but hold small essentials like a credit card, key, or energy gels for long runs. The leg openings are spacious, allowing for a full range of motion, and an adjustable drawstring secures the waistband for a customizable fit. Want to hit the road at the crack of dawn or at night? No sweat; reflective detailing improves visibility in dark or dim light, making early morning or evening runs safer.

Recent findings suggest that I appreciate the 4-inch length, given I prefer more coverage, but a 2.5-inch length is available if you prefer a shorter fit. WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, is also a fan of the fit and vast color palette. “They never ride up or move around, which is hard to find in a running short,” she says. With tons of colors and sizes to choose from, you can't go wrong.

In a recent development, new Balance is a top brand in the running world, and the RC Short is one of my faves. It runs slightly massive, but I love the extra breathing room during a sweat session.

Sources indicate that the lightweight, flowy construction uses the brand’s quick-drying tech fabric (a polyester and spandex blend) to wick moisture from the skin. The breathable design promotes tons of airflow, creating a cooling effect while I run—especially ideal during scorching hot summer runs.

The seamless, interior lining reduces chafing and irritation, while the waistband features an adjustable drawstring to customize the fit. It’s also not too tight—some liners can feel like you’re wearing a diaper (hate). As for storage, there’s a back pocket for securing small running essentials and even tiny snacks like a granola bar when you’re on the move.

Sources indicate that WH style contributor Lily Wolhner also appreciates this loose style for various workouts. “My favorite part about this short is that it’s never clingy, so it doesn’t ride up the thigh or need constant re-adjusting while you’re working out,” Wolhner notes. “I’ve worn it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout, as well as an hour-long cross-training workout—I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it.”.

By the looks of the elastic waistband, I expected it to dig into my skin—wrong. It felt comfortable, although it’s important to note this short does run significant, so I suggest sizing down.

Industry observers note that we love a two-for-one, and this short from Brooks is ideal for both trail running and running at the gym. It has light compression with a built-in tight liner that doesn’t sacrifice mobility.

Sources indicate that if you want a no-frills pair of shorts at an affordable price point that will stand the test of time, the Under Armour Play Up 3.0 belongs in your running gear collection. The lightweight knit fabric made from smooth polyester has an anti-pill finish for extra durability, and is impressively comfy. Plus, it hides embarrassing sweat stains post-run, despite the slightly thicker material.

It has been revealed that the waistband uses a wide elastic band that provides a secure fit without any adjustable features. However, I find it still fits roomy and allows for a full range of motion.

It has been revealed that it includes deep side pockets but no enclosure, so I don’t recommend stashing anything super important besides fuel, like energy gels. I wear it the most for shorter, mid-distance runs and whenever I want to add a pop of color—it has 21 color options!

Sources indicate that I usually don’t gravitate toward compression shorts since I don’t like feeling constricted, but the Athleta Salutation Stash 5-Inch Short offers the perfect amount of tightness. According to recent reports, another huge selling point? The fabric’s UPF 50 protection, which prevents UV radiation from scorching your thighs. Industry observers note that tracksmith’s Van Cortlandt Shorts combine retro styling with a performance-driven design that makes them a winner both on and off the track. Running shorts with sweat-wicking fabric are the way to go, Katz says. Based on testing, it’s best to avoid cotton since it doesn’t dry nearly as fast and clings to the skin when wet.

Sources indicate that it’s crucial to determine what kind of rise and inseam you desire. High-waisted running shorts offer more coverage and tummy control, while a mid-rise waist sits right at the hips. Ultimately, what you find most flattering for your body type is the best option.

Sources indicate that the inseam is the length from the crotch to the bottom. A longer length will show less skin but may disrupt the range of motion, while some running shorts favorites, like the Lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short, offer a 2.5-inch option if you like a mini fit.

As for an interior liner or compression, this will make running shorts fit more snugly. “Compression is a matter of preference, but the goal in this material is to boost recovery,” notes Katz. If you want a less constrictive fit, it’s probably best to avoid that feature.

Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and indicates it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators indicates Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and indicates it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Sources indicate that at 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

Sources indicate that the SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

FHP stated the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

According to recent reports, this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it states Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

According to recent reports, how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Industry observers note that most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

So Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s key to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

Industry observers note that there’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

It has been revealed that this is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a new record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

Sources indicate that this is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

According to recent reports, tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

It has been revealed that we’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

Industry observers note that if FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

According to recent reports, we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An AI-assisted search of NASA's archived telescope data has uncovered two possible planets, with preliminary checks by a professional astronomer recovering both signals.
  • 24 report, OpenAI detailed how two amateur astronomers used its Codex and Astra tools to search observations of millions of stars for previously overlooked planetary candidates.
  • Kevin Bond, an OpenAI engineer, used Codex to develop software that detects recurring declines in stellar brightness, a potential indication of a planet passing in front of its host star.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An AI-assisted search of NASA's archived telescope data has uncovered two possible planets, with preliminary checks by a professional astronomer recovering both signals.

In a recent development, in a Nov. 24 report, OpenAI detailed how two amateur astronomers used its Codex and Astra tools to search observations of millions of stars for previously overlooked planetary candidates.

Kevin Bond, an OpenAI engineer, used Codex to develop software that detects recurring declines in stellar brightness, a potential indication of a planet passing in front of its host star.

It has been revealed that bond combined existing detection methods into a program that deployed two AI agents. One identified promising signals, while the other subjected those findings to further examination.

Running the software against archived observations of approximately 100,000 stars from NASA's Kepler Space Telescope produced more than 200 signals, including 10 associated with previously confirmed planets.

Vishal Gajjar, an astronomer at the SETI Institute, independently recovered two of Bond's findings.

According to recent reports, the first involved a relatively cool star, KIC 5689121, whose brightness declined every 13.8 days. OpenAI mentioned the signal was consistent with a potential planet approximately 2.4 times Earth's diameter. The second, KIC 6691030, exhibited recurring dips every 4.8 days, suggesting a potential planet smaller than Neptune.

OpenAI claims SETI Institute astronomer Vishal Gajjar recovered both dips in the same Kepler data Kevin Bond searched.

Each repeat interval gives astronomers a pattern to test in follow-up observations.

Recent findings suggest that the traces illustrate timing with schematic dip shapes and depths. The causes of both dips remain unresolved.

Sources indicate that both traces use a common 28.5-day window from an arbitrary starting point. Their dips are spaced at OpenAI’s reported approximate intervals of 13.8 and 4.8 days. Positions are rounded to the nearest SVG coordinate.

The traces illustrate timing with schematic dip shapes and depths. The causes of both dips remain unresolved.

“Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.”.

While Bond focused on Kepler's archived observations, another amateur astronomer, Ethan Byrd, used OpenAI's Astra to examine telescope data covering approximately 19 million stars.

Byrd developed two searches, including one targeting planetary candidates within habitable zones, where atmospheric conditions could allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface.

Recent findings suggest that his initial search identified 49 candidates. Byrd has submitted one to researchers working on NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission, and two others are awaiting submission.

Astronomers have used artificial intelligence to identify planets for years. In 2017, NASA revealed the discovery of Kepler-90i using a neural network trained to recognize planetary signals in telescope observations.

General-purpose AI tools now let amateur astronomers develop their own detection software and search vast archives for signals earlier searches may have missed.

However, recurring declines in stellar brightness can also result from eclipsing stars or fluctuations in telescope instruments.

Astronomers could investigate Bond's candidates by observing their host stars at the predicted transit intervals and measuring whether gravitational forces from potential orbiting planets cause detectable stellar movement.

Establishing whether either signal represents an undiscovered planet could take months or years, OpenAI said.

  • Recent findings suggest that the first thing I noticed: the fabric.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SUMMER MAY BE behind us, but that doesn’t mean your swim trunks need to go into hibernation. If you’re planning to escape the cold for somewhere sunny this winter, a good pair should be in your suitcase. The beauty of men’s swim trunks is that they can be worn in or out of the water, doubling as the ultimate beachside bottoms or everyday shorts. The best swim trunks for men today have a moisture-wicking and quick-drying fabric, four-way stretch for mobility, a flattering length, and an athletic fit. Finding the right one for you can be a challenge, which is why we're here to help. Our team of fashion editors spent the past year trying and testing swim trunks to find options that blend comfort and style.

Over the past four years, I’ve tested more than 20 different pairs of swim trunks—everything from legacy surf brands to buzzy newcomers—but Fair Harbor’s have consistently exceeded my expectations. This pair nails that trifecta of being stylish, functional, and worth the price.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing I noticed: the fabric. It’s a cotton-poly blend that feels smooth and broken-in right out of the gate. It doesn’t feel like any of that stiff, swishy, overly synthetic feel you get with most swim trunks. I’m usually quick to write off built-in liners altogether, but the BreezeKnit liner changed my mind. It feels more like a supportive pair of boxer briefs than the usual scratchy mesh. It’s snug (but comfortable on the crown jewels), breathable, and, most importantly, it doesn’t ride up or chafe. I’ve worn it for full beach days in Puerto Rico—swimming, walking, grabbing lunch—and never once felt the need to adjust.

The 7-inch inseam hits just above the knee on me, giving it a clean, tailored look. It’s an easy middle ground that works whether you’re getting in the water or just wearing it as your default summer short. There’s enough stretch in the cotton-polyester fabric that I never feel restricted. Plus, it comes in seersucker versions, solid-colored options, and other unique patterns. The hidden zipper pocket stashes a key or card without them slipping out, and the side pockets don’t balloon up in the water—something a lot of trunks still get wrong. It’s not a substitute for a gym short, but the fabric dries quickly for other oceanside activities.

Read More: The Best Shorts for Men.

I can’t get enough of the R&R Trunk's timeless style, functional fabric, and flattering fit. I love the no-fuss design with a tailored cut that’s not too baggy or slim. Coupled with the flexible waistband, the fit looks great on most body types. It’s available in two inseams–5.5 and 7.5 inches. The latter provides enough coverage and hits a couple inches above the knee for most men (our universal style recommendation for shorts). Though I wore the shorter length on the beach during my stay in Miami because it indicates off my summer leg gains.

Sources indicate that rhone’s athleisure performs just as well as it looks. I’ve sweat-tested the R&R during beachside runs and volleyball games, and found that its odor-fighting fabric kept me feeling fresh. The mesh liner kept my family jewels locked in, without cutting off circulation. A few editors on our style team who have the R&R trunk say that the liner really does have a second-skin like quality. That’s probably because the polyester blend fabric is stretchy, which felt more comfortable than Lululemon’s (also great!) Swim Short. These durable features also mean the R&R Trunk doubles as a decent gym short if you’re in a pinch, and saves you one less thing to pack for a tropical vacation. We love that it comes in 11 colorways, but if you want to go classic, you can’t go wrong with the Electric Blue or Navy option.

Read more: Best Running Shorts for Men.

According to recent reports, the absence of liner offers a comfortable commando style, which is why I prefer a pair like this one from Lululemon. I don’t have to be bothered with any mesh material that feels restrictive or scratchy against my crown jewels—I can just slip it on and head into the water. I also love that the minimal design doesn’t scream “swim trunk”, so I can go from brunch to the boardwalk or the pool without having to do an outfit change. It passes as an everyday short, which is exactly the kind of versatility I want in the summer. The polyester-elastomultiester fabric has so much stretch, it performs just as good—if not better—than most of my gym shorts.

Sources indicate that I’ve worn this pair for pickup volleyball and quick workouts, and they move with you instead of clinging or sagging out. It also dries fast and doesn't get that heavy, waterlogged feel after a swim, which makes a huge difference if you’re posted up poolside for a while. The 7-inch inseam is short enough to show some quad, but long enough that it still feels put-together if you’re grabbing a drink after. On my 5’8” frame, it lands a couple inches above the knee with a clean, tailored look—not too baggy, not too slim. If you’re taller, it’ll read a bit shorter and sportier; shorter guys get that ideal mid-thigh cut without going full retro.

After testing Proof’s Performance Swim Trunk, we found that it’s easily the most durable short on this list. Our editors appreciate the polyester-spandex blend fabric, which is stretchy, quick drying, and nearly tear proof. We’ve sported this during tropical hikes and extreme water sports, and found that the Performance Trunk held up to just about anything mother nature threw at it. We like the moisture-wicking liner, which is actually more comfortable than Rhone’s R&R short, but we did find it didn’t dry as quickly as Rhone’s short, and is a bit thicker than we’d prefer. Still, those are minor quibbles for a swim trunk as functional as this one.

According to recent reports, looks-wise, the Performance Trunk isn’t the most stylish of the bunch, and it’s not meant to be. It’s available in six solid colors and two inseam options, all of which have a no-frills design. Though we have to say, because of its barebones aesthetics, the Performance Trunk looks a lot cleaner than your typical bulky hiking short. Proof markets this as a multipurpose trunk that doubles as a gym short, and after putting it through the paces, we agree with that claim. While it’s not as breathable as Ten Thousand’s award-winning Interval Short, Proof’s stretchy fabric moves easily through all sorts of workouts.

For your next vacation, you need a dressy swim trunk that can look great at the beach, bar, or restaurant. Enter this one from Bather, which has a plaid-like pattern with complementing tones of maroon and blue. This makes it more polished than your typical swim shorts, so you can easily pair it with a simple polo or the brand’s matching camp shirt and sandals for a foolproof, lunchtime fit in your arsenal. I’ve worn it to a five-star hotel’s restaurant and then straight to the pool for a mid-day cocktail.

The waistband rests gently on the waist, but you can adjust the fit using the drawstrings. Unlike the scratchy net-like liners in cheaper swim trunks, the nylon-spandex blend is silky and irritation-free, so I could wear it for hours and be comfortable. Plus, the 5.5-inch inseam flatters tall and short guys alike. In terms of functionality, the pockets are super deep for your sunglasses or wallet, while one in the back snaps shut for extra security.

It has been revealed that fair Harbor offers so many great trunks, we couldn't help but to feature the Anchor Short, too. It's available in a variety of solids and prints, but we're substantial fans of the red stripe option, since it has a cool ‘80s vibe that pairs well with laidback T-shirts, tank tops, and more. This style also comes with the BreezeKnit liner—Fair Harbor's soft, supportive alternative to traditional mesh liner found in swimwear. It provides a snug and comfortable feel, while keeping you cool as ice.

Industry observers note that unlike other picks on this list, The Anchor Trunk is available in three inseams. The 6-inch inseam is great for guys who want to show off their hard-earned leg gains this summer. The 8-inch inseam hits the sweet spot between casual and polished, a safe bet if you're unsure which to go for. And the 10-inch inseam is the longest option, ideal for those who prefer a bit more coverage. Plus, its relaxed (not baggy) fit keeps this from veering into Reno 911! territory.

Read more: Best Hybrid Shorts for Men.

Ralph Lauren’s classic style is the most versatile of the bunch—it works as a swim trunk, a casual short, and even a workout short. I’ve worn it for early runs along the boardwalk, knocked out quick leg circuits on vacation, and then jumped straight into the water without needing to change. The 5.75-inch inseam gives it a shorter, more athletic cut that feels mobile and unrestrictive, especially when you’re moving. But its trimmer, more style-forward look makes it clean enough to pass as an everyday short.

It’s made from a lightweight polyester-elastane blend that dries rapidly and has just enough stretch that you can bend down or twist at any turn. The mesh liner feels breathable and supportive, unlike traditional swim trunks. And because the silhouette is sleek and the design is minimal—save for that signature embroidered pony—it pairs easily with a tee or button-down, making it a true wear-all-day option for beach trips, resort hangs, or any summer day that doesn’t stick to one lane.

It has been revealed that sure, this is the most expensive option on our list, but we think Orlebar Brown's Bulldog Trunk packs serious style that’s worthy of its higher price point. The polyester-elastane fabric is designed with a textured stripe pattern, which is very sharp and unexpected—something most guys would shy away from, so you’ll probably be the only guy at the pool rocking it. I wore mine to the beach in Costa Rica, and no one had anything remotely close to this pair; only baggy boardshort-like types.

Sources indicate that this one lands mid-thigh at a 6-inch inseam, which is the golden length for most men. It’s not as stretchy as the Rhone pair, but you’re not rocking this for comfort; the Bulldog is all about quiet luxury. When I’m not in the water, I wear it with just about any solid polo or camp shirt for a five-star resort fit. Plus, the gold fasteners on the waist add extra style points, and just look super plush.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for something more surf-specific, the California-based brand best known for its laid-back, surfer aesthetic delivers the Cruise Boardshort. It’s cut from a lightweight polyester-elastane blend that dries impressively fast, making it ideal for long days in and out of the water. The scalloped leg—where the hem curves slightly upward at the outer thigh—gives you a greater range of motion and a subtle retro-sport look. It’s one of those design tweaks that looks cool but also improves mobility.

According to recent reports, it’s built to stay put. The double drawcord waistband adds extra security, so even when you’re getting knocked around by waves or caught in a strong current, you’re not worrying about your trunks slipping. It’s a small but clutch feature if you’re actually swimming, surfing, or doing anything more active than lounging.

According to recent reports, patagonia used a creative, cloudy effect across its lengthy boardshort that looks like sun-faded tie-dye you’d find on a well-traveled surf trip. It’s stylish enough to stand out amongst a sea of guys in basic trunks. Like Vuori’s option, this pair falls right above the knee, providing more coverage in case your shorts ride up as you get out of the water. I’m 5'8" and the 18-inch outseam fits pretty long on me, so the fit is more flattering for taller guys around 6’ feet. If you want things even longer, the brand also offers a 21-inch version that hovers over the knee.

Industry observers note that despite the trimmer leg, the cut never feels restrictive—it’s got enough room to move without baggy. It’s made with a lightweight polyester-spandex fabric that has a slightly sturdier structure than most of the swim trunks, but flexes whether you’re paddling out or diving a volleyball. I found it dries down quickly between dips, and the double looped waistband ensures it stays secure.

Patagonia’s Baggies Short has proven its durability on everything from multi-day hikes to back-to-back swimming sessions. Our guys have worn this trunk for backpacking through rugged trails, jumping into rivers, and air-drying in the sun—day after day—without wearing them out. The tough nylon fabric resists abrasion from rocks, sand, and saltwater, while the water-repellent coating helps it dry quickly.

Unlike traditional slanted pockets that can balloon up in the water, this pair has mesh openings inside, so the water flows out and doesn’t weigh you down. Despite dozens of uses and hours in the ocean, we haven’t seen these trunks fade, fray, or lose shape. Our fashion editors found they pair nicely with a string of T-shirts and sneakers for coffee pick-ups or quick grocery runs.

Sources indicate that sometimes, swim trunks with loud designs can be too in-your-face, but Mack Weldon went easy on this pair. It’s decked out with a dotted gradient pattern that adds a visual pop, without looking tacky. Our editors have worn this with a white polo to balance things out, and works as a foolproof fit for beachside lunches. We especially like the fit: it’s relaxed, but slimmer than the Bather swim trunks for a dressier vibe.

Sources indicate that like most of the swim trunks on this list, this version is made with a polyester-spandex flex that offers a lot of mobility. We could maintain a full range of motion through running, squatting and walking. During our testing, the mesh liner didn’t irritate our family jewels either. In fact, it was one of the more comfortable liners on the list.

In a recent development, if you're performing heavy activities in swimsuits, consider doing without liners. Board shorts, for instance, aren't made with liners for more wiggle room and comfort. Otherwise, liners should fit snugly, but should never be too tight or pinch your skin. Built-in mesh liners provide extra support to your down-there and keep everything in place as you move. Since they're mesh, they're also breathable and quick-drying.

Shorts are getting shorter, and so are swim trunks. But you don't have to chase trends. Typically, around 7 inches in inseam length is a universally flattering fit that hits a couple inches above the thigh. Though if you want to show off your quads, you can't go wrong with a 5-inch inseam, either. If you're looking at outseam lengths, 14-inch is more fashion-forward, 17-inch is a casual mid-length, and 20-inch is as full coverage as you can get without wearing pants.

If you're swimming, surfing, or just moving around a lot in bathing suits, Stafford advises stretch as a must-have factor, since it allows a great fit and range of motion in and out of the water.

Waistbands should fit comfortably on your body, and a drawstring may help you to adjust the waist size if needed. We recommend a full-elastic waistband with a drawcord because it ensures you keep your trunks on, even if you’re diving from the high dive. If you’re going for a snap closure, just make sure it’s not too tight with the ability to unsnap after one beer.

It has been revealed that to find the best swim trunks for men, our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, spent the past five years testing more than 100 swim trunks in a variety of settings. For instance, we went whitewater rafting in Proof's performance shorts, swam laps in Rhone's R&R short, and sported Orlebar Brown swim trunks at the beach. From there, we evaluated these swim trunks based on their style, fit, price point, performance in and out of the water, and versatility to make the final top picks.

In a recent development, bonus points if they doubled as athletic shorts or hiking shorts. Specifically, we looked for styles that are not trendy or trend-chasing; instead, our picks of the best swim trunks have a flattering fit, provide a ton of value at reasonable price points, and come in styles that will look great years from now.

The 12 best swim trunks for men tested by our style editors below are all quick-drying, comfortable, and look great. Whether you're planning to wear these to the beach, poolside, or to your weekend lunch, the best swim trunks for men have you covered.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, cotton is a no-go—it gets way too heavy when met with water. Our fashion team recommends lightweight synthetic fabrics since they dry promptly and are usually fade-resistant to the sun and chlorine. These synthetic fabrics are ideal for underwater wear because they won't get hefty and pull you down when drenched in water.

In a recent development, poly with the addition of stretch (Lycra, elastane) material is the most common with good reason—more comfortable, forgiving. Some brands use nylon instead of poly because it absorbs less water and does not get heavy as the waterproofing wears off over time, but nylon does not (take color) dye as deeply and vibrantly as poly.

Industry observers note that choosing the right color and print for men's swim trunks boils down to personal style, skin tone, body type, and occasion. If you prefer a more classic and versatile look, solid colors like navy, blue, or olive are excellent choices that can easily transition from the beach to casual outings. If you want something a bit more eye-catching, subtle patterns like stripes or small geometric prints add personality without being too loud. For those who like to stand out, bright colors, tropical florals, or retro-inspired prints make a strong statement, especially on an island.

Sources indicate that your skin tone can also guide your choice—fairer skin tones tend to work best with earth tones and pastels, while medium to tan skin pairs well with rich blues, corals, or reds. Darker tones can pull off almost any color, but bright neons and strong contrasts pop especially well. Body type plays a factor too—shorter guys might benefit from vertical stripes or a shorter inseam to create a lengthening effect, while taller guys can balance their frame with medium-to-long inseams and bold patterns. Athletic builds look great in solid colors and tailored fits that highlight their shape, whereas stockier builds might find that darker shades or micro-prints create a more streamlined look.

Lastly, think about where you'll be wearing swim trunks. For pool parties and resort vacations, playful prints and vibrant hues add to the fun, while sporty designs with color-blocking work well for active beach days. If you're looking for swim trunks that can double as everyday shorts, muted tones or subtle patterns offer the most versatility. Ultimately, the best choice is whatever makes you feel confident and comfortable.

XRP Bulls and Bears to Get 3x ETFs Soon

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (361 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • exchange-traded funds would give investors a way to bet on XRP in either direction, with one targeting three times XRP's daily return and the other targeting three times its inverse.
  • If XRP gains 5% in a single day, the bullish ETF would target a 15% gain, excluding fees and expenses.
  • If XRP loses 5% in a single day, the bearish ETF would target a 15% gain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two proposed U.S. exchange-traded funds would give investors a way to bet on XRP in either direction, with one targeting three times XRP's daily return and the other targeting three times its inverse.

If XRP gains 5% in a single day, the bullish ETF would target a 15% gain, excluding fees and expenses.

If XRP loses 5% in a single day, the bearish ETF would target a 15% gain.

However, investors betting on the wrong direction could lose approximately 15% of their investment in a single day.

The next update is scheduled for Nov. 30. Following a recent amendment submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the registration statements for these ETFs are now scheduled to become effective on Monday.

The issuer has repeatedly delayed the effective date. It remains to be seen whether the funds will start trading anytime soon.

The filing covers a total of eight ETFs, including bullish and bearish funds for Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL) and XRP.

Even if XRP's price remains unchanged over multiple trading days, both ETFs could record negative returns.

Since the ETFs rebalance daily, it's notable to remember that when the price changes direction, the next day's percentage return is calculated based on the investment's value after the previous trading session.

Let's say XRP rises from $2 to $2.20 on Monday and then drops back to $2 on Tuesday. If you hold XRP over these two days, you'll break even.

However, if you invest $100 in the bullish ETF, your position would close Tuesday at approximately $94.55, assuming the fund achieves its daily target and excluding fees and expenses.

It has been revealed that if XRP increases by 10% from $2 to $2.20 on Monday, the bullish ETF would target a 30% gain. Your initial $100 investment would now be worth $130.

For XRP to return to $2 on Tuesday, it would need to fall by approximately 9.09%.

The bullish ETF would therefore target a loss of roughly 27.27% on Tuesday. But that loss would be calculated against your $130 position, leaving you with approximately $94.55.

Of course, the bearish ETF wouldn't fare any better.
