📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

PROTEIN POWDER CAN be a powerful supplement when used correctly, like creatine or a multivitamin. But finding the right one for your needs is a massive task in an overcrowded protein market. Studies show protein powders can help build lean muscle and promote optimal recovery, making them a widely sought-after supplement. It’s hard to find an easier way to make progress toward your daily protein goals than by taking a few big gulps of a high-protein smoothie. But protein powder is not just a vehicle for hitting your protein goals—many powders also contain other beneficial nutrients, like iron, calcium, fiber, and sometimes even vitamin D.

Sources indicate that there are multiple types of protein powder to sift through, the most common being whey protein. Whey protein is derived from cow’s milk and is the most widely consumed type of protein powder. In addition to whey, you’ll find casein protein (also derived from cow’s milk but slower to digest than whey), and plant-based proteins (rice, pea, hemp, pumpkin seed, or a blend of these).

Recent findings suggest that overall, the best protein powders keep it simple: They boast a solid macronutrient profile and taste great. While there are other factors that should be in consideration throughout your search (i.e., third-party testing, type of protein, and price), if you stick to those two basics, you’re likely to find a powder you can easily and consistently implement into your daily routine. Do you need to slam a protein shake as soon as you finish working out? No.

Sources indicate that other lists out there have too many picks, in our opinion, and we're only looking to share with you the very best of what we've found. Our in-house testers have put dozens of protein powders through the blender (and shaker) for years, not months, and dubbed these six as their favorites. The same could be said for the expert nutritionists we consulted with, like Jordan Sullivan, who's worked with UFC champions like Israel Adesanya and Alex Volkanovski. If you’re on the hunt for a reliable protein powder and want the tedious testing work done for you, read below for our top picks for the best protein powders.

I'm a NASM-certified nutritionist who has spent years covering the intersection of fitness and nutrition. I started with input from the Men's Health editors, including Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, and Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. Our team spent hundreds of hours testing products, interviewing registered dietitians, medical doctors, fitness professionals, athletes of all kinds (some of whom shared their insights below), and our own Advisory Board.

According to recent reports, the testing pool started with the top-rated and bestselling protein powders on the market, then was cut down from there. The products that made it into this guide undergo third-party testing, hold an NSF, USP, or Informed Sport certification, and contain standardized forms of protein in clinically studied, safe amounts.

Sources indicate that we considered every nutrition label, ingredient list, price, and many reviews from certified buyers. We made and drank hundreds of post-workout protein smoothies as part of our examination process. The list below represents our thoughtful picks of the very best protein powders to help with your gains in 2026.

Sources indicate that the brand name doesn’t lie here—Transparent Labs lists all ingredients clearly on the label and unlike some other protein brands, it doesn’t include ingredients you can’t pronounce. Without fillers or artificial ingredients, you’re left with the important stuff: 28 grams of whey protein isolate, only 1 gram each of carbs and fat, and just 130 calories. You’ll also find a touch of three micronutrients (we’re talking less than 9 percent of your recommended daily value), calcium, iron, and potassium. Another perk? This protein powder is sweetened with stevia extract, so you won’t find any added sugar here.

Men’s Health Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, tested the product personally and claims, "it was a refreshing surprise to try a product without unnecessary junk in it. The high-protein content of this product let's me hit my intake goals with ease, and also tastes great.".

Recent findings suggest that all that mentioned, Transparent Labs Whey Protein Isolate is sourced from grass-fed dairy, so it won’t be suitable for vegans. And a protein that’s as clean as this one comes with a higher price tag. While the average protein powder on this list costs closer to $1.50 per serving, TL will run you $2.00 a serving. But for us, Transparent Labs’ high protein content per scoop and lack of filler ingredients is well worth the extra 50 cents.

When looking for the best protein powder for athletes of all ages, we want two things: First, we need an all-around solid product that boasts ample protein. Second, we need a product that is thoroughly third-party tested and certified safe for competitive athletes. Thorne Whey Protein Isolate ticks both of those boxes, and it also happens to taste great, according to Thorp.

Thorp didn’t just test this product for this review. "Thorne is one of the supplement brands I have used the most, and its protein powder has been a mainstay in my routine," he notes. And for good reason: It boasts 21 grams of bioavailable whey protein isolate, and just 4 grams of carbs, 1 gram of fat, and 100 calories. With such a low calorie count, you can also mix this powder with other ingredients (fruit, peanut butter, etc.) to create a hearty, protein-packed smoothie.

"The taste of the chocolate flavor is smooth, and blends well with any fruit or additional nutrition you want to add, or just on its own with water or milk," Thorp says. "There is a mild amount of sweetness, but it doesn’t overpower. The result is pretty pleasant as far as taste.”.

While the flavor and macros are great, it’s worth noting that this protein does contain gums, which some athletes may avoid. Thorne also costs a bit more than average at $2.17 per serving—but if you’re a competitive athlete looking for a certified product, that extra cost should provide the assurance you need.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve been hunting for the right protein powder for a while, it’s likely you’ve come across Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard 100% Whey in the process. Optimum Nutrition is one of the most widely known (and used) protein brands—take it from Thorp, who initially started his fitness journey taking Optimum Nutrition Gold Standard. One of the biggest draws for newbies just testing the waters (and financially savvy folks in general)? The price point.

Depending on the jug size (the bigger you go, the cheaper the cost per serving), your price per scoop can be as low as $1.06 with the highest you’ll pay for a scoop from a smaller container being only $1.54. How does the brand keep the cost lower than the market average? Thorp explains, “It's not a pure whey protein isolate (it's a blend) and depending on your stomach, you'll realize this fast.” (Sensitive stomachs may want to lean toward a less dairy-heavy whey isolate.).

But if the whey isolate, whey concentrate, and hydrolyzed whey protein blend is not an issue for your digestive system, this is a great straightforward option featuring 24 grams of protein and 5.5 grams of BCAAs. Just make sure you’re mixing with milk or in a smoothie as we did find this powder to have a synthetic aftertaste in testing when we mixed it solely with water.

In a recent development, if you’ve been to your local health foods store, you’ve likely seen Orgain Organic Plant Based Protein Powder. Thorp can attest, "I first started using Orgain when I went vegan for a few years," he notes. "This was back when there weren't as many vegan protein powder options as there are now. I liked how accessible it was, through both Amazon (usually at some sort of discount) and at my local Whole Foods.".

Aside from being easy to attain, Orgain is also made with a plant protein blend, which provides a full amino acid profile—a trait sometimes difficult to come across in vegan protein powders. The taste is also reliable. Thorp found the flavor lighter than some of the other protein powders he has tested in his over 10 years working in the supplement space. He also noted that it blends better than most vegan powders with a smooth and creamy mouthfeel, rather than a gritty one.

Sources indicate that though this powder packs 21 grams of protein, it also contains 15 grams of carbs and 3.5 grams of fat, which is higher than your typical whey protein. While this may not be ideal for those on a cut, Thorp offers a different perspective: "While it has more carbs and fats than others, that could be a positive for anyone looking to really supplement their diet in a larger way. [This nutrition profile] makes it a more satisfying drink." And with that, it’s notable to note that a full serving is two scoops, so you may need to blend with a little more water or milk than normal to make sure the texture is not overly thick.

Sources indicate that if taste is your number one priority, Dymatize ISO100 should be your number one pick. MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., also stands by this protein powder. "It's nutritional profile is great," he states. "That's why this Dymatize is the only protein I use.".

“The flavor is top-notch. [Dymatize] is among the most consistently best-tasting wheys, regardless of the specific flavor," indicates Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey.

Ritchey also noted that her sensitive stomach had no qualms with this hydrolyzed whey protein isolate, which is a testament to the product’s hydrolyzed form. Whey protein isolate is whey protein that has already been broken down into smaller peptides for easier digestion, but hydrolysis takes that processing a step further—studies show the absorption level is even higher in hydrolyzed whey isolate.

With 25 grams of protein and only 120 calories, this is a great lean protein option. Just note that there are artificial flavors and gums, which some may avoid for digestive purposes.

If you’re vegan, lactose-intolerant, or just want to add a little variety to your protein sources, Transparent Labs is pulling through. Transparent Labs Organic Vegan Protein is our favorite vegan protein powder for two reasons: One, it is a blend of pea and rice protein, which studies have shown offers a complete protein (similar to a whey) with a full amino acid profile. You'll find if you decide to go with just a pea protein product, you'll likely still be recommended to take it with a rice product as well. And two, it boasts 15 percent of your recommended daily iron, which studies show some vegans may be deficient in.

This vegan protein also packs a higher protein content per serving than most vegan powders—24 grams compared to the more typical 20 grams. Thorp tested Transparent Labs Organic Vegan Protein and thinks it’s a great option not just for vegans, but for anyone looking for a different source of protein. "This is one of my favorite proteins around, and it [just] happens to be vegan, for any of those living by that diet or [who are] lactose intolerant. Also, if your diet already has a lot of dairy in it, using this protein powder can help to diversify your intake," he notes.

It is also worth noting that though Transparent Labs Whey Isolate comes in a wide variety of flavors, the flavor options for the pea protein and rice protein products are more limited—just chocolate or vanilla.

Read More: Best Vegan Protein Powders.

Recent findings suggest that there are three main types of protein powder to consider: whey protein, casein protein, and plant-based protein. You’ve probably seen whey protein the most—it’s derived from cow’s milk and comes in the form of whey concentrate, whey isolate, or hydrolyzed whey. Whey concentrate is the least processed form of whey protein, and therefore, contains the most dairy. Whey isolate is processed to remove most of the dairy, and hydrolyzed whey is processed even further for the best absorption of the three, according to studies.

Casein protein is also derived from cow’s milk, but it is much slower to digest than whey protein. Some people even take casein at night, so it has time to process as they sleep, according to some studies. Plant-based protein is derived from plant-based sources like rice, pea, hemp, pumpkin seed, or a combination of these. It can be higher in carbs and a touch lower in protein because of this, but proteins made of a blend of plant sources typically provide a similar nutritional profile to whey proteins. There is no right or wrong answer when it comes to the type of protein you should seek out—it just comes down to what you’re best able to implement into your fitness routine and daily lifestyle.

In a recent development, A good protein powder typically offers anywhere from 20 to 30 grams of protein per scoop. Plant-based powders often sit on the lower end of this range with whey and casein being on the higher end. You’ll want to consider how much protein you want from your shakes vs. your whole food meals. If you’re looking to use a protein powder as part of a smoothie for a meal replacement, you’ll want a powder closer to 30 grams of protein, according to studies. If you’re just looking to use a protein shake as a snack, that 20 grams range will work just fine.

While protein is the main character, fats, carbs, and calories are also important considerations. If you’re looking to build lean muscle, you’ll want a protein powder that’s low in all three—it’s surprisingly easy to find a protein powder with three or fewer grams of both fat and carbs, especially whey isolates and hydrolyzed wheys. If you're bulking it could even be tempting to try a protein powder that's high in carbs, fats, and calories, but you will never accomplish the same quality of nutrition you get out of actual food. Better to focus on getting a quality protein powder and grab a quick real meal when you can.

While all of the products we talk about on this list are third-party tested, this certification is a big factor to consider when hunting for supplements. Many supplements don’t provide third-party testing (protein powders included), and since supplements aren’t FDA-regulated, there’s no way to know if what’s on the product’s label is actually what’s in the product without third-party testing. Be sure to take this into account when considering any supplement purchase.

Your average protein powder will cost anywhere from $1.00 to $2.00 per serving, with most falling right in the middle around $1.50 per serving. The more expensive powders are typically cleaner, boasting all-natural ingredients, no additives, a higher protein content, and thorough third-party testing. The less expensive options may contain more artificial ingredients, have a lower protein content, and/or offer no third-party testing. Compare prices and ingredients across this list (and throughout the market) to find the best value product for your lifestyle and budget.

In a recent development, while most athletes focus on the massive three (protein, fat, carbs), micronutrients should not be overlooked—especially if you follow a specific diet (like vegan or keto). Protein powders can be a great source of other nutrients like iron, calcium, vitamin D, and potassium. These micronutrients may be more important to those who don’t get them as much from their regular diet (vegans, for example, often don’t get enough iron in their regular meals). But according to studies, it’s also a good idea to pay attention to these ingredients to ensure you’re not consuming an overkill amount of any particular micronutrient.

In a recent development, if you’re finding it difficult to get enough protein in your daily diet, protein powders can help. They’re a convenient way to help hit your protein goals—easier than downing four or five chicken breasts a day, at least.

In a recent development, getting enough protein in your diet can help you build lean muscle and recover better after your workouts. This is thanks to amino acids (the building blocks of protein), which help stimulate muscle protein synthesis. Studies show during muscle protein synthesis, the body uses these amino acids to repair muscle tissue after your workouts—i.e. your body’s way of building muscle.

Sources indicate that if you’re following a solid workout regimen, protein powders can be a great way to sneak in some additional protein on top of your whole food diet. Studies show protein can help you stay fuller for longer, too. But remember that protein powders are meant to be a supplement, meaning you should still be getting most of your protein from whole food sources.

Protein powders can contain additional ingredients—like artificial flavors or sweeteners, fillers or gums, allergens, and/or added sugars—that some customers may try to avoid. The key with these types of ingredients is moderation.

While artificial flavors and sweeteners haven’t been proven harmful in moderation, there isn’t enough evidence on how consuming them consistently can impact long-term health. Gums and fillers should also be consumed in moderation as they can cause digestive complications. Like artificial flavors/sweeteners, there’s also a broader concern over the long-term effects these ingredients may have, but more research is needed. Added sugars—ingredients like table sugar, high-fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, honey, molasses, and fruit juice concentrates—are also best in moderation, as they’re high in calories but offer no real nutritional value. Studies show added sugar should make up less than 10 percent of your daily calories.

It has been revealed that allergens—like gluten, dairy, or nuts—are the only ingredients you’ll want to avoid entirely if you have a specific food sensitivity. Dairy is probably the most relevant one with protein powders as most whey and casein products do contain dairy (even if it’s in trace amounts).

Recent findings suggest that the Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority. The reason isn’t quantum computers.

It has been revealed that protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters. The quantum threat has always been a hardware problem, and hardware problems announce themselves years in advance because somebody has to build the machine. The AI version is a math problem. A sufficiently capable model could find a structural shortcut in the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin, and it would need no special hardware to do it.

Sources indicate that researcher Justin Drake raised the scenario in October. In a worst case, he mentioned, existing signatures could become vulnerable within months.

Industry observers note that an Anthropic mathematician named Levent Alpöge posted a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced with an unreleased version of Claude, along with a formalized proof archive. Nobody has verified it. It doesn’t break elliptic curve cryptography and nobody is claiming it does. What it does is demonstrate the capability class Drake was describing, roughly a month after he described it.

Sources indicate that axios reported Tuesday that more than two dozen people familiar with internal discussions at OpenAI and Anthropic say employees worry their most advanced unreleased models may never be safe enough to release. The concerns named include reward hacking, models that hide or misrepresent their reasoning, and systems capable enough to find weaknesses in the safety measures their own developers built. OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed Sunday that labs agree on shared limits on how far they train models.

Sources indicate that the plan replaces elliptic curves with hash-based cryptography, which rests on fewer structural assumptions about mathematics. It touches how users authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how layer-2 data gets verified. Drake proposed pulling the deadline from December 2029 to December 2028. Ethlabs withdrew its faster-block-production proposal from the Hegotá upgrade to free up engineers. The Foundation has deployed AI agents to hunt bugs in its own infrastructure, which is a reasonable response and also an admission about where the advantage right now sits.

In a recent development, wedderburn’s own framing: it’s harder than the Merge, and there’s less time. He also acknowledged that moving faster makes it easier to ship bugs.

In a recent development, bitcoin is on the same road. Blockstream’s Jonas Nick published a security analysis of SHRINCS last week, the apparent frontrunner to replace Bitcoin’s signatures, with sizes running from 548 bytes to 5,777 against today’s 64 to 71.

It has been revealed that so the AI threat is looming (and accelerating), but the two largest crypto assets have teams that are responding. You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even challenges with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

In a recent development, “Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” claims Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.).

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” notes Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

Industry observers note that to find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

Recent findings suggest that while everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Sources indicate that martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

Industry observers note that at over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

Read more: Best Home Office Chairs.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that crucial feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

According to recent reports, during testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she states, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”.

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

According to recent reports, this electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she notes. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Sources indicate that her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

It has been revealed that this walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Industry observers note that not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you proposal to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.).

Sources indicate that at the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

In a recent development, it’s notable to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

According to recent reports, we should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. #213421. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data shows a speed problem

Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data shows a speed problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • Industry observers note that four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Industry observers note that four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

According to recent reports, those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

It has been revealed that the second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

In a recent development, tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

Sources indicate that the Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

It has been revealed that tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

In a recent development, two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider remarked they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Recent findings suggest that those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

Industry observers note that the Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

Sources indicate that in the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

Engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

In a recent development, the Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

What the data reveals is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data reveals at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five XRP Ledger accounts supplied 72% of one day’s trading volume in XRP against Ripple USD (RLUSD), according to XRPL.to.
  • For a test of the next day’s order book, CryptoSlate selected the five addresses that led the Nov.
  • It has been revealed that funded RLUSD in the first 100 buy offers fell from about 63,925 to 8,805.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five XRP Ledger accounts supplied 72% of one day’s trading volume in XRP against Ripple USD (RLUSD), according to XRPL.to.

For a test of the next day’s order book, CryptoSlate selected the five addresses that led the Nov. 25 session in fills of at least 1,000 XRP, then simulated removing their buy orders.

It has been revealed that funded RLUSD in the first 100 buy offers fell from about 63,925 to 8,805. In the model, the matching pool, a standing reserve of both assets, took most of a 100,000 XRP sale after the removal. A seller would receive about 3.3% less RLUSD than with the full sample.

The last XRP/USD trade on Kraken was $0.94935 when the ticker was checked at 13:07:24 UTC on Nov. 26. On the ledger exchange itself, XRP/RLUSD accounted for 84% of all volume measured in XRP over the seven days covered by XRPL.to’s reconstruction.

In the 24 hours ending at 01:30 UTC on Nov. 25, XRPL.to’s reconstruction counted 25,801 fills moving about 6.3 million XRP. Traders took resting offers from 142 accounts or traded against the automated pool.

According to recent reports, the biggest account, whose ledger address starts with rpiFwLYi, supplied 41% of executed volume. Together, the five largest supplied 72%, and the pool accounted for 3%.

A replay through the public trade history endpoint yielded 6.32 million XRP and counted 25,712 fills for the same window, 89 fewer than the published tally.

According to recent reports, the index can group multiple executions into one transaction row. In one row covering 525.58 XRP, the validated transaction showed about 514 tokens went to one account’s buy orders and about 12 tokens to another’s.

To test whether concentration persisted, CryptoSlate used XRPL.to records and split combined fills using validated ledger changes.

The comparison covered same-pair fills of at least 1,000 XRP in three 24-hour windows ending at 01:30 UTC on Nov. 24, 25 and 26. The same five addresses, selected by Nov. 25 qualifying volume, accounted for about 71%, 88%, and 79% of qualifying volume, respectively.

The address starting with rpiFwLYi led the middle session, with about half the qualifying volume. An address starting with rURtT5MM led the sessions on either side.

That left the same group with a large share in all three windows even as the leading address changed, and the turnover includes trades in which the addresses gave or received XRP.

The two sides of the XRP Ledger’s order book draw on different inventories. A resting order to buy XRP is funded in RLUSD, which the seller receives. A resting order to sell XRP draws on the seller’s inventory.

The relevant depth for a seller is the RLUSD that buyers can deliver at the displayed prices.

At validated ledger 108584374, which closed at 13:09:20 UTC on Nov. 26, the first 100 buy offers could take about 67,549 XRP at the displayed prices.

It has been revealed that excluding buy offers from the five large-fill leaders left room for about 9,302 XRP in that same sample. The funded RLUSD in the sample fell about 86%.

It has been revealed that the matching XRP/RLUSD pool held about 1.99 million XRP and 1.89 million RLUSD. The model applied its standard 0.315% fee and allocated each portion of the sale to the better available price.

The test held the remaining offers fixed and used only the sampled book and the direct pool, with deeper orders, replacement orders, and additional fees outside the simulation.

In the model, a 1,000 sale returned 947.96 RLUSD with the full order sample and 947.87 without the five addresses’ buy orders. At 10,000, proceeds slipped from 9,474.85 to 9,470.90 RLUSD. At 100,000, proceeds fell from 94,197.18 to 91,050.74 RLUSD.

The pool took about 32,451 XRP in the first case and 90,698 after the orders were removed.

A fixed-ledger comparison of how the order book and automated pool divide the same modeled sale.

Modeled proceeds fell about 3.3% as the pool took roughly nine-tenths of the sale after the orders were removed.

In a recent development, the removal case excludes buy offers from the five makers that led the November 25 sample of fills of at least 1,000 XRP. The model holds the other sampled offers and pool starting balances fixed and excludes deeper, fresh and other-market orders.

Sources indicate that each bar totals 100,000 XRP. Order-book volume is that total minus modeled pool volume. Amounts and proceeds are rounded to whole units. The source inputs are the first 100 buy offers and the matching pool at validated ledger 108584374, with the pool’s standard fee.

Recent findings suggest that the removal case excludes buy offers from the five makers that led the November 25 sample of fills of at least 1,000 XRP. The model holds the other sampled offers and pool starting balances fixed and excludes deeper, new and other-market orders.

The pool’s price worsens as sellers draw down its RLUSD reserves, which is why a large trade can clear and still return less.

  • Sources indicate that berg’s new Netflix film dramatizes the stories of football players John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), who traded the NFL draft for military service.
  • In a recent development, the Mosquito Bowl underlines the devastating impact WWII’s casualty count had on an entire generation of young athletes, and the film unites its twin focuses of war and football by their mutual sense of brotherhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DIRECTOR PETER BERG had never made a World War II movie before The Mosquito Bowl, but he certainly knows a thing or two about football. The director of Friday Night Lights has returned to a world of cocksure young players with their whole lives ahead of them in dire need of rousing their morale—only now it’s the true story of the football game between two World War II Marine regiments at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944. There’s another connection: both The Mosquito Bowl and Friday Night Lights are adapted from books by author Buzz Bissinger.

Sources indicate that berg’s new Netflix film dramatizes the stories of football players John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), who traded the NFL draft for military service. After enduring years of the Pacific campaign, they realize how valuable the team spirit and camaraderie of football can be as the Battle of Okinawa looms ahead of them.

In a recent development, the Mosquito Bowl underlines the devastating impact WWII’s casualty count had on an entire generation of young athletes, and the film unites its twin focuses of war and football by their mutual sense of brotherhood. The deeply felt connection between soldiers is the lifeblood of historical war films; when done convincingly, a squad’s well-earned devotion and loyalty add rich melodrama to the action. Brotherhood is just as compelling when it is subverted—like the respect felt between soldiers on opposing sides, or when hardened, broken combatants struggle to express the empathy and compassion they feel. The best war movies know that brotherhood endures after the fighting stops, but in different forms—softer, stranger, when it’s hard to reconcile the memories of war with a world that continues as normal.

To mark the Thanksgiving release of The Mosquito Bowl on Netflix, we ranked the most gripping and rousing war films about brotherhood.

It has been revealed that an ensemble of actors you'd typically see in a "Young Stars of Tomorrow" profile immerse themselves in a U.S. Navy SEAL platoon and recreate a real-time Iraq War firefight that co-director Ray Mendoza was a part of. Opening with the platoon jubilantly dancing to "Call On Me" streamed through their base's crappy internet, Warfare quickly adopts a stripped-back and meticulous play-by-play of how one slice of warfare was actually experienced. You get a sense of brotherhood from the practiced, reflexive interactions between SEALs, and their interdependence also helped build the film, as Mendoza and co-director Alex Garland drew from the testimonies of his fellow soldiers when writing the script. The stylistic choices—like a thundering sound mix and infrequent use of satellite photography—add an extra layer of tension to Warfare's depiction of courage under fire. It’s one of the most visceral movies in recent memory about modern war.

Industry observers note that before he brought us high-octane visions of robot cops and ambitious showgirls, Paul Verhoeven directed a handful of smash hits in his native Netherlands, including this Golden Globe-nominated war epic about the diverging fates of Dutch students during the Nazi occupation. Led by a supremely dashing Rutger Hauer, Soldier of Orange begins in 1938 and follows the wartime trajectory of Erik Lanshof, an initially neutral but increasingly principled aristocrat who protects his Dutch Resistance friends and distances himself from fascist collaborators. Before long, his entire school group has pledged one type of loyalty or another. Observed over a period of time, war reveals everything, and Erik’s blossoming heroism emerges as a result of his friendships all changing—for better or worse.

Recent findings suggest that forgive us for taking a creative approach to the headline so early in the list: Hell in the Pacific features no battles or squadron camaraderie, and takes place on a deserted island with only two characters—an American pilot (Lee Marvin) and a Japanese army captain (Toshiro Mifune)—who don’t understand a word the other person states. Even without comprehension, the American and Japanese soldiers find a hundred ways to rile each other up, including shock tactics, sabotage, pranks, and even makeshift imprisonment. Gradually, they realize each other’s company is the strongest connection to their starving humanity available to them, even if they’re affected in a way they can’t explain. Free from the rhetoric and politics of war, Marvin and Mifune play men who slip into a state of brash, stubborn childishness, and a brotherly kinship forms in spite of their inherent opposition.

It has been revealed that clint Eastwood and Steven Spielberg sound like an odd pair to collaborate on a war picture, but Eastwood’s pared-down, melancholic visual style is a terrific fit for this post-Band of Brothers war movie. Flags of Our Fathers wasn’t received as positively as its Japanese-language companion film Letters from Iwo Jima, but it’s a robust and affecting watch—splitting its runtime between the overwhelming Battle of Iwo Jima and its aftermath, where three soldiers celebrated as the iconic “flag-raisers” spent the final year of the Pacific Campaign on a spiritually draining propaganda tour. Flags of Our Fathers takes the essential themes of war cinema—brotherhood, sacrifice, heroism—and juxtaposes them with the United States military manufacturing their own national images and narratives in real time. The tension between the brutal experience of being a brother-in-arms and the sanitized version promoted by war’s survivors makes for a powerful watch.

It’s as if director David Ayer (Suicide Squad, Bright) made a WWII movie to hammer home two points: tank warfare was a nightmare, and soldier hazing was way more hardcore than what you see in Band of Brothers. In the final months of the war in Europe, Wardaddy (Brad Pitt) rolls his bloody and battered tank unit slowly toward Berlin, and the arrival of fresh-faced pencil-pusher Norman (Logan Lerman) gives the hardened squad a chance to berate and bully the newcomer about all the ways he is soft, and war is hell. As their fellow brothers-in-arms are increasingly blasted apart into viscera, Wardaddy’s take-no-shit squad bolsters their unsentimental unity, and each of the five traumatized brothers rely on each other to watch their back and keep them sane on a frontline that might as well be the border to hell.

Spike Lee’s bracing film about the scars of Vietnam takes a familiar concept—a jaded band of veterans who try to pull off a heist—and spins it in a thorny, unpredictable direction. Four older Black veterans (led by an intense, captivating, and Oscar-snubbed Delroy Lindo) return to ‘Nam to recover the CIA gold their squadron hid during the war—aside from a delayed payday, it’s also the ultimate memorial of their late squad leader Norman (Chadwick Boseman). Marked by years of bitterness and PTSD, the “Bloods” retrace their steps while juggling painful reflections on how the war left them angry and guilty. When they're ambushed in the jungle and have to pick up guns again, we're reminded that Lee is never satisfied sticking in one narrative mode for too long, but the jagged catharsis of cranky, once-loyal soldiers confronting their wounds is far more visceral to watch.

When Private Alex (Harry Styles) says, “We're regimental brothers, mate,” in the belly of a fishing trawler on Dunkirk Beach, he’s not acting nobly—he’s making the case for throwing a soldier he thinks is German (he’s actually French) to the Nazis surrounding them. So much of Christopher Nolan’s war film about the perilous evacuation of Allied troops from France’s northernmost beaches centers on division: soldier feuds, breakdowns in communication, and a nonlinear narrative that takes place over a week or an hour depending on who’s in front of the camera. But Dunkirk’s staggering disaster and survival action builds to an overwhelming climactic sense of unity. Across every mini-arc and timeline, Nolan highlights us countless pairs of soldiers, pilots, and civilians who stand together as symbolic brothers.

After the famously gnarly and disorienting D-Day beach landing sequence—which has influenced every WWII action movie since, including The Mosquito Bowl—Saving Private Ryan settles into the most iconic band of brothers story outside of… well, Band of Brothers, co-created by this film’s director and star. Tom Hanks is the grouchy uncle leading a reluctant squad to rescue Private James Francis Ryan (Matt Damon) from the front lines after his brothers were killed in action. The squadron's trudge through France is fueled with banter, grumbling, and the type of resentment that stews between siblings who hate when someone receives special treatment. Steven Spielberg’s gift for balancing movie-star gravitas and off-the-cuff charisma is on full display in the ensemble, but no gruff, hot-tempered soldier has a response to Private Ryan's justification for not returning to his mom: “Tell her that when you found me, I was here, and I was with the only brothers I have left.”.

In a recent development, the only war film on this list to be set before the 20th century and at sea, the Napoleonic Wars-era Master and Commander has a reputation for being a “dudes/gentlemen rock” classic: the reputation still holds up. Under the command of Captain Jack Aubrey (Russell Crowe), the HMS Surprise wages war against a French frigate that taunts the crew across the seas. Majestic naval battles aside, much of Master and Commander has a warm hangout tone, focusing on the kinship between Aubrey and ship’s surgeon Maturin, their interest in classical music and botanical science, and revelrous suppers in the captain’s quarters. It's impossible to watch Peter Weir’s sea epic and not pine for the brotherly loyalty (maybe not the seasickness or cannonball attacks) that Aubrey inspires here. Nothing will make you feel the romantic thrill of adventure like Master and Commander.

Pick your favorite scene from The Deer Hunter: the riotous wedding party, the spontaneous Frankie Valli singalong over a game of pool, or the exacting game of Russian roulette played by prisoners of war. They each shine a light on the ordinary, working-class brotherhood that was completely transformed by the Vietnam War. This Oscar-winning epic builds complex, traumatized characters (played by Robert De Niro, John Cazale, and Christopher Walken) who reckon with never being able to experience their relationships and community in the same way again. The Deer Hunter paints such a disturbing and fragile picture of the “before and after” of Vietnam, as each brotherly bond becomes charged with alienation and despair. Notorious for its multiple “death game” sequences, The Deer Hunter excels in making its harrowing portrayal of war and PTSD genuinely heartbreaking.

In a recent development, one of the best things to come out of legendary Hong Kong filmmakers John Woo and Tsui Hark falling out was the future director of Hard Boiled and Face/Off leaving the iconic A Better Tomorrow series to make this searing war story. Beginning in the late ’60s, it focuses on three close friends (Tony Leung, Jacky Cheung, Waise Lee) whose smuggling ambitions dunk them headfirst in the brutality and desperation of the Vietnam War. Bullet in the Head blends the epic sweep of Upcoming Hollywood war epics (Apocalypse Now, The Deer Hunter) with Woo’s “heroic bloodshed” toolkit, which meant electric action spectacle and bold, tragic melodrama. An underrated operatic beast in Woo’s stacked filmography—not to mention a personal one, as Woo used the film to express his reaction to the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre—the action is always in service of a high-stakes tri-friendship that can only take so much passion and betrayal before the treasured brotherhood breaks.

Sources indicate that rory Doherty is a critic and journalist based in Edinburgh, Scotland. His work can be found at British GQ, Vulture, Inverse, AV Club, and other publications. He can be found on Twitter/X at @roryhasopinions.

Latest Update: Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system.
  • Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.
  • Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

Industry observers note that that matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

Recent findings suggest that the savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” stated Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

According to recent reports, by combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

Industry observers note that that’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning fresh fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

According to recent reports, include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

Good way to think about the whole system. So what exactly does Don not-Quixote have against windmills?

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

Raving in Your 40s, 50s, and 60s? These Women Say It’s the Best Self-Care They’ve Found

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning.
  • In a recent development, that’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo.
  • It has been revealed that manson isn’t an outlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning. She’s loved music her whole life and was always drawn to EDM, but marrying and having kids young left little room to explore it. Then, three years ago, her husband died, and she began thinking about how short and precious life is—and decided it was time to push herself to try new experiences.

In a recent development, that’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo. She was nervous, but spent the night dancing, and left with newly introduced friends and a newfound confidence. “I felt uninhibited,” she says. She’s attended more than 20 raves since.

It has been revealed that manson isn’t an outlier. Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns. And a number of them are finding relief on the dance floor.

Industry observers note that A 2025 study in Psychology of Music surveyed 136 women ages 40 to 65 about why they’re involved in EDM experiences. The overwhelming response was that raving was a meaningful part of their mental well-being—an outlet for stress, a source of connection, and a rare place to escape the demands of everyday life, according to the survey.

“There is a rise in older people attending electronic dance music events, raves, clubs, parties, festivals,” says Alice O’Grady, PhD, a professor of applied performance at the University of Leeds, who co-authored the Psychology of Music study. “The motivations for women going are pretty much characterized as the same as they are for any age: the love of the music, the ability to socialize with existing friends, the atmosphere of the environment, and the sense of community.” Put simply: These music events are plain fun.

The EDM scene is no longer the epitome of youth culture, O’Grady adds, and it’s become more socially acceptable for women to embrace this genre of joy as they get older. That shift may reflect changing attitudes about aging, with women potentially feeling less constrained by traditional expectations about how they’re “supposed” to spend their time as they age. Social media has also made it much easier to discover niche music scenes, while a growing focus on mental health, movement, pleasure, and community may be encouraging women to seek out experiences that just make them feel good.

According to recent reports, the older you get, the harder it can be to find a place where you can be playful, spontaneous, and fully present with other people. For some, the rave scene provides exactly that. “You've got more responsibility, more commitments,” O’Grady states. “You want that escape, you want that ability to connect through music and immerse yourself in an environment that allows you to be expressive and just shake off some of those roles that older women carry.”.

Sources indicate that samantha Hillery, 43, started raving in her 20s as a way to let loose and have fun. But as life got busier with work, family, and kids, she stopped going. Years later, while searching for fun things to do in her area with friends, she came across Bingo Loco, a high-energy party with EDM, dancing, confetti, and—yes—bingo, and found her way back to it.

Now, Hillery gives herself permission to step away from the endless list of adult responsibilities. “As we get older and super busy with our lives, we forget how fun we maybe used to be, and it seems like something that was so far in the past,” she says. “But when you’re able to go out and rave surrounded by a bunch of friends and people that just want to have a good time, you remember that part of you isn’t lost.”.

Industry observers note that for some, keeping up with friends also becomes more challenging as you age and enter new eras of your life. Social obligations often come second, competing with work schedules, children, relationships, and other obligations, says Madison Liddle, LMHC, a licensed psychotherapist at Madison Liddle Therapy and co-founder of The Practice Co, a co-working space for therapists. At a music event like these, though, spontaneous connection is built into the experience.

In a recent development, hundreds or thousands are gathered around the same music, moving to the same rhythm, creating an immediate sense of belonging. It’s a concept called collective effervescence, which is “a feeling of joy and connection when a group of people are in a shared space doing a shared thing,” Liddle explains. “Social connection is a really strong determinant of health as we age, and raving offers an opportunity to create and be in community with people with shared interests.”.

Getting out and meeting latest people is the main reason Manson is so attracted to rave culture—she’s found the crowds to be welcoming and friendly. “Life can become quite small if you don't push yourself,” she indicates, alluding to feeling alone after her husband’s passing. “I enjoy meeting people, I enjoy conversations. I'm not good at home in my own tech giant—I need socialization.” Dancing with new friends is the way to do that, and it keeps her feeling energized.

In fact, in Manson’s experience, the EDM scene has seemed remarkably friendly to people of all ages and backgrounds. O’Grady agrees: “Women need spaces that are inclusive, welcoming, and accessible, and the rave scene actually does that quite well,” says O’Grady. You’ll feel a sense of belonging, like you’re part of something bigger than yourself, even if you’re there alone, she adds. The music creates an instant common language, while dancing alongside friends and strangers turns what could be an individual activity into something meaningful and collective.

According to recent reports, the physical perks of dancing are well documented. It strengthens the cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and cognitive systems, as WH previously reported. It can also improve coordination, balance, and stability, which becomes especially key with age. But it can boost your mental health too, mainly because it helps you stay present. When you’re fully focused on what you’re hearing, feeling, and doing, there’s less room to get caught up in the mental replaying and worrying that can fuel stress, Liddle says.

In fact, many participants in the Psychology of Music study described dancing at raves as a way to ease anxiety, depression, and low moods, notes co-author Alinka Greasley, PhD, a professor of music psychology at the University of Leeds. Anxiety can keep the mind focused on what might go wrong, while depression can make the present feel flat.

According to recent reports, raving, by contrast, demands attention in a different way. Instead of sitting with your thoughts, you’re listening to loud, immersive music, dancing to the beat, and anticipating the next drop, Liddle explains. That physical engagement helps interrupt rumination and creates a sense of clarity that lasts beyond the dance floor; it can help clear your head.

In a recent development, alex Daly attended her first EDM show at 40 after her partner, who’d been going to raves for years, encouraged her to come along. A year later, raving has become a central part of her wellness routine. If she’s having a stressful week and doesn’t have an EDM show on her calendar, she immediately starts looking for one. “Once I’m in the crowd, I get into a flow state, and moving my body to the beat really helps me process my emotions,” indicates Daly, now 41. “Dancing helps me stop ruminating, get out of my head, and back into my body.” For a few hours, there’s simply less room for the mental noise of everyday life. In a way, it’s like the pounding beat is a reset button you can dance to.

It has been revealed that of course, rave culture has long been tied to recreational drugs like MDMA, which can bring on feelings of euphoria, connection, and stress relief. That link hasn’t disappeared. Some of the women in the Psychology of Music study noted they took drugs, often to keep their energy up for dancing, while others went purely for the music and the movement.

According to recent reports, however, drugs weren’t what gave the women a sense of belonging, the study uncovered. “That's very much already there from their perspective,” Greasley indicates. “The drugs are more to do with [increasing] energy levels and also the marrying of the drugs and the music. Many women called it a spiritual experience to be in ecstatic states whilst dancing to the music.”.

Karen D., 62, who asked that her last name be withheld because she discusses her drug use, sees it the same way. She started going to raves in her early 50s with her second husband. While she partakes in recreational drug use, she also knows people who attend raves completely sober. For her, the bonding comes from dancing with like-minded people who are all just happy to be there.

But Karen acknowledges that drugs heighten those feelings and add to the mental health boost she gets from raving. “I feel like my brain’s reconnecting in ways that it has forgotten how to connect,” she states. “I can get down with what’s going on in my life at times, and it completely transforms me into a much more positive person.”.

It has been revealed that wellness advice in your 40s, 50s, and beyond is often the same advice over and over: protect your sleep, drink less, manage stress, and stick to a routine. But in contrast, this group of ravers finds genuine self-care in the act of staying out late, dancing for hours, and disrupting those prescribed wellness rules. “In this world where everything is so optimized and planned and scheduled, there is something that we lose in terms of fun,” claims Liddle, noting that raving brings it to the forefront. The key is to accept the occasional trade-off—less sleep in the name of mental health benefits—and to strike a balance between partying and recovering.

Manson has attended a couple of Daybreaker events, which are morning, sober parties and raves, often starting around 6 a.m. Early parties like these are becoming more common. O’Grady adds that more women DJs are putting on earlier demonstrates with the attitude of: “We all want to get together, we all want to have a dance, but we want to be in bed by midnight.”.

However, Manson prefers later indicates because she finds that’s when more traditional EDM is played. But staying up until 4 a.m. at these events has been a bit of a learning curve, so she tries to limit her events to one per weekend. “The enthusiasm's there, but I'm not prepared to spend so much time recovering,” she notes. “Once is great, it does what I want it to do. It makes me feel good. I get to connect with people that I enjoy spending time with.” She prioritizes sleeping in the next morning, and just rests the next day if she needs to. Then, she can still go to the gym and take long walks during the week. (She doesn’t work anymore, so she has more flexibility to rest.).

Industry observers note that despite the missed-out-on sleep, Karen D. finds that rave life rejuvenates her. “If I've been away at a festival for a weekend, I come back very tired because I need more sleep,” she says. “However, I do feel refreshed somehow—more clearheaded.”.

But she still makes sure to still get seven hours of sleep if she goes to bed late, so then she can still fulfill her responsibilities at home, like taking her grandson to school. The tradeoff is also worth it for her, and in fact, going to raves inadvertently benefits her wellness routine. It “really helps motivate me to do weight training, to go running, to do all these wholesome recognized exercises, because I want to stay well to be able to go and dance [until] 3 o'clock in the morning,” she says.

Rave culture is no longer just for younger people, and women in midlife are soaking in every ounce of fun, freedom, community, and release. “They don't want to be defined by their age, but more importantly, they don't want to be restricted by it,” indicates O’Grady. “Saying, ‘I want to dress up in my sequins, I want to put my face on, I want to go and have a dance, I want to stay out all night and shrug off my responsibilities for a little while, I want all of that and why shouldn't I?’”.

For Manson, getting ready is part of the appeal, and she’s collected a variety of vibrant, fun outfits to go out in. “It's almost like creating a bit of an identity, which I'm quite enjoying,” she notes. At this stage of life, raving has given her a way to reinvent herself.

Sources indicate that midlife can chip away at a woman’s confidence and leave her feeling overlooked. Raving pushes back on that by giving women a place to be bold and seen. As Karen D. puts it, “Women of my age can often disappear or become invisible, and it's almost the opposite of that.”.

Since her husband’s death, Manson has made a point of pushing herself to try new things. Raving has given her lasting memories, a fresh outlook, and a crew of friends who aren’t ready to stop dancing anytime soon. “I live with the feeling that life’s very short and precious,” she says, “so seize the moment.”.

In a lending market where borrowers are using most of the funds, repayments or fresh deposits can free up tokens for another withdrawal.

On eligible vaults, Morpho also offers an in-kind exit that can return some EURCV to the wallet and convert part of the redeemed amount into a direct position in a lending market.

Two Nov. 26 liquidity readings show how much of the largest position the vault could cover in a hypothetical full exit.

Vault liquidity controls how many tokens can leave. Direct issuer redemption has its own eligibility checks and cash deadline.
